title: Agentic Governance and Adversarial Verification for Policy-Constrained LLM Healthcare Appeal Generation
content: Claim denial management costs U.S. healthcare approximately $260 billion annually in administrative overhead. Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can produce fluent clinical text, but single-agent architectures fail in high-stakes healthcare: they introduce unsupported clinical details and lose the logical structure of hierarchical payer policy. We propose AGVF (Agentic Governance and Adversarial Verification Framework), a multi-agent architecture for medical-necessity appeal generation under explicit policy and evidence constraints. AGVF models appeal synthesis as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) over five agents: policy formalization, evidence retrieval, gap analysis, adversarial critique, and gated synthesis. We prove that refinement over a fixed policy constraint graph monotonically reduces evidence-deficiency and terminates with either a complete satisfying frontier or a localized evidence gap. A deterministic citation- grounding gate prevents assertions without admissible evidence from entering shared state. We provide a reference implementation and validate it on 1,000 synthetic appeal cases parameterized from de-identified public hospital discharge data. The validation confirms zero citation-grounding violations across all AGVF cases and monotone deficiency reduction in every episode; ablating the gate raises violations to 100%, confirming it is load-bearing. The study uses no real patient records and does not measure clinical efficacy. AGVF thus contributes a theory-backed agentic architecture and verified reference implementation for policy-constrained LLM generation in healthcare.

title: American Nobel laureate receives Polish citizenship
content:

American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros, whose father emigrated from Poland after World War Two, has received Polish citizenship. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him to give him the good news personally.
Ambros, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on microRNA, revealed earlier this year during a visit to Warsaw that he was seeking Polish citizenship and hoped to help strengthen Poland’s scientific standing worldwide.
Jesteś obywatelem najlepszego państwa na świecie!🇵🇱❤️ pic.twitter.com/cBDfMDS3Ax
— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 16, 2026
“I have great news for you: you are a Pole, you have a Polish passport,” Tusk told Ambros during the call. “You are a citizen of the country that is the best place on Earth – at least I believe that.”
Ambros told Tusk that he was “honoured” to receive the news. Speaking later to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), the scientist said that he was “very grateful to Prime Minister Tusk and to Poles for awarding me Polish citizenship”.
“I hope that my having dual citizenship – American and Polish – will honour both my father’s Polish roots and the opportunities that America created for him and me.”
Ambros, who is already chair of the scientific council of the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences, also expressed hope that there would be “additional opportunities to help improve the international position of Polish science, especially in the field of biomedical research”.
Ambros’s father, Longin, was born in 1923 in what was then the village of Dordziszki in Poland but which, after postwar border changes, is now Dordishki in Belarus. He later attended high school in the city then known as Wilno, and which was part of Poland, but is now Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania.
During World War Two, Longin Ambros was deported to Nazi Germany and used as forced labour, before being liberated at the end of the war by American forces, who then employed him as an interpreter.
In 1946, Longin emigrated to the United States, where he settled on a farm and raised a family. Victor was one of eight children and the first scientist in the family.
American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros has announced that he is seeking Polish citizenship in order to honour his family “and all those who fought and survived so that I could exist today”
He also wants to contribute to the development of science in Poland https://t.co/70uXhh1fj6
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026
There has been a growing trend in recent years for foreigners to seek Polish citizenship. There are three paths for those wishing to obtain it.
The first is through Polish ancestry. People with a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who lived in Poland after 1920 and never lost their citizenship can apply to have their status as a Polish citizen officially confirmed.
Last year, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Poland, received Polish citizenship, describing it as the “honour of a lifetime”. His Oscar-nominated 2024 film A Real Pain was set entirely in Poland.
Eisenberg is currently starring in a new state campaign promoting Poland abroad, along with football star Robert Lewandowski and supermodel Anja Rubik.
Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US.
The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026
The second route is for foreign residents in Poland who meet requirements relating to their length of residency, language skills and personal situation to apply to the governor of the province where they live.
The third is by applying directly to the president, who has discretion to grant citizenship without any specific legal requirements being met. Applicants are expected to show personal ties to Poland and explain their reasons for seeking citizenship.
One recent example was Russian-born speed skater Vladimir Semirunniy, who fled to Poland and was granted citizenship last year by President Karol Nawrocki. This allowed him to win a medal for Poland at the recent Winter Olympics.
Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago.
Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026
Last year, Poland granted citizenship – either through provincial governors or directly from the president – to a record 19,135 people. Over half of the recipients were Ukrainians, who constuitute by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. In 2024, the figure stood at 16,342.
However, the Polish government is currently working on measures to make it tougher for foreigners to obtain citizenship, including increasing the minimum residency period and requiring applicants to take a test proving they are integrated. They would also have to sign a declaration of loyalty.
Applications to confirm citizenship through descent have also risen sharply, in particular among Israelis, many of whom have roots in Poland.
Last month, rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski announced that he was also applying for Polish citizenship with a view to representing and winning medals for the land of his ancestors on the international stage.
Rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski has announced he wants to represent Poland, the country of his ancestors.
His best 100m time of 9.89 seconds is the 9th fastest in the world this year and over a tenth of a second faster than Poland's national record https://t.co/S2tZsiSAhh

title: Perhaps Malaysians are a lot kinder than we think
content:
A middle-aged Chinese woman from an NGO walked into the newsroom, seeking help.
A journalist of Indian descent was assigned to write the story — that of a young Malay girl who urgently needed medical attention.
This story, recounted by FMT executive chairman Nelson Fernandez at a forum recently, would have just been another account of how Malaysians help each other.
But this was different. People of all races came together to answer a call for help by a Chinese, disseminated by an Indian to help a Malay.
Within hours of FMT publishing the story, up to RM150,000 had been pledged, taking little Diya Amanda on her first step towards a normal childhood.
But for Fernandez, it was just another day at the office.
The Malaysia we keep saying we want is already here.
Nobody ever needed a campaign or matching T-shirts to foster unity. Nobody asked who prayed where or what box they ticked on a form.
This was simply a child who needed help.
And people came forward.
Back in 1982, Paul McCartney and Stevie Wonder sang a lovely song about “Ebony and Ivory” living together in perfect harmony. If black and white piano keys could exist in harmony, surely human beings could figure it out too.
More than forty years later, humanity is still working on it.
We, Malaysians, have spent decades talking about unity. We have slogans, campaigns and speeches about it. We have probably printed enough banners about togetherness to wrap around the country several times over.
Yet one of the best demonstrations of Malaysian unity happened without anybody needing to announce it.
Just like the song, maybe harmony doesn’t require every key to sound the same.
I don’t think Malaysia suffers from an absence of harmony. Perhaps we suffer from not seeing enough of it.
That matters because the stories we repeatedly hear about one another influence the nation we are a part of.
If Malaysians constantly encounter one another through anger, suspicion and confrontation, eventually it becomes easy to believe we are fundamentally divided.
This is why Fernandez’s argument about journalism matters beyond journalism.
He wasn’t suggesting difficult stories shouldn’t be told. Nor should they be.
He was asking for something harder: that conflict does not become the only lens through which Malaysians see one another.
We should be able to disagree fiercely without dehumanising others. We should be able to defend what we believe without humiliating someone who believes differently.
And when we report what divides Malaysia, we should not forget the stories that reveal what still holds us together.
That responsibility isn’t just journalists’ anymore.
Every one of us carries a tiny newsroom in our pockets. We decide what gets shared, forwarded and viral-ed.
Fernandez said something else at the New Muslim Community Conference in Kuala Lumpur, that stayed with me:
“Everyone talks about religion, but no one talks about love, compassion and kindness.”
Love. Compassion. Kindness.
Three words that might seem soft beside politics, race, religion and power.
But as I wrote in my previous article, we have grossly misunderstood softness and strength.
It is easy to be kind to people who agree with us and who are similar and familiar. It takes something stronger to extend that kindness to someone who isn’t.
Perhaps Malaysians do not need to agree on everything and maybe agreement was never the point.
Harmony isn’t everyone singing the same note. That’s unison.
Harmony requires difference.
Ebony and ivory don’t create music because they overcame their differences. Their differences are the point.
Malaysia isn’t so different. A unique colourful country like ours was never going to be one note.
I believe we should stop trying to make everyone sound the same and become better at hearing one another instead.
That’s where harmony begins.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

title: 'I'm forever grateful for my girl's donated heart'
content:
'I'm forever grateful for my girl's donated heart'
- Published
Ahead of Organ Donation Week, two mothers whose children were involved in transplants share their stories from either side of the experience.
Seven-year-old Evie is thriving.
She is doing well at school, enjoys playing with friends and is keen to give everything a go, her mother Chloe Green says.
But for her daughter to be doing so well today, another family had to go through the unimaginable pain of losing their child.
When she was three years old, Evie needed a new heart.
The toddler from Middlesbrough spent 16 months in hospital in Newcastle being kept alive by a Berlin Heart, a mechanical pump which she had to be permanently attached to.
Evie featured in a project by Consett-based photographer Debbie Todd, taking before and after pictures of children awaiting life-saving organs.
Sadly, Debbie says, not all the children got their "after" picture.
Evie's wait was so long she ended up having three "before" photos taken, images treasured by Chloe as showing the journey her daughter had to undertake.
Chloe, 31, and her husband David, 38, would swap places by her hospital bedside, juggling looking after her with work and caring for their other child, Evie's brother Theo, who is a year older than his sister.
Chloe says she tried to stay optimistic, focusing on "small wins all the time", but her mindset changed when Evie had to be attached to the machine.
"I was watching her dying," Chloe says. "Suddenly my priority was 'we need a new heart'."
She understood what that meant for any potential donor.
"I did feel I was in a moral quandary," Chloe says. "It comes with a lot of guilt.
"Of course you are not wanting someone else to die, but the doctors said we could only think of what we needed for Evie's treatment plan, you have to have that boundary."
They were waiting for another family to do an "amazing thing", Chloe says, and the appreciation never fades.
"Whenever I reflect back or see Evie hitting a milestone, I think of that [donor] child," she says.
"I almost feel like they are part of our family, they are coming along with us."
The donated heart was a "perfect match" for Evie and has "done so much for her", Chloe says.
She acknowledges that may not fully comfort the donor's family but might give them some peace to know.
Chloe does not know who the donor was but has written a letter to their family, there for them to read should they ever choose to.
"If I could speak to the donor's family, I would just be forever thanking them," Chloe says.
"We would love to share everything about Evie's life if they were willing to, but of course it has to be their choice.
"It would just be constant gratitude. I am forever grateful to them."
Anna-Louise Bates knows what it is like to receive such a letter.
In 2015, her husband Stuart and seven-year-old son Fraser were killed when they were hit by a car near their home in Talbot Green in south Wales.
Because he died at the scene, Stuart, who had signed the organ registry and wanted to be a donor, was unable to be one.
But Fraser's heart, lungs, liver and kidneys were given to three other children and an adult, with his heart going to a young twin boy from Hartlepool called Roman.
"I won't forget the first letter I ever received from his mum," Anna-Louise says. "How the loss of my boy had allowed hers to grow.
"To know Fraser lives on has given me so much hope, it was like they didn't die in vain.
"Life is a gift and the biggest gift you can give is life."
She said milestones such as Fraser's recent 18th birthday were "incredibly difficult", but hearing of Roman enjoying life and having "10 years' worth of memories and love" gave "some comfort".
Anna-Louise founded Believe Organ Donor Support, to encourage people to think about organ donation and discuss it with their loved ones.
At Stuart's insistence, she and her husband had the "icky" conversation just two weeks before the crash, and Anna-Louise is so grateful they did.
It meant in that "24 hours of hell", the questions around organ donation were the "only time I didn't have to think", she says.
Knowing her husband's wishes and how her son was meant she felt confident to agree to donate, with the lives Fraser saved "a testament to the big heart he had".
She has in the years since thought about it from the recipient's point of view, she says, about how a parent might feel knowing a "young child passed away for you to have that organ".
"The way I reconcile that is I am just pleased Fraser's gift has allowed a child to live on," she says.
"He gave the greatest gift and especially because this was so close to Christmas, he gave the gift of life that he could no longer be part of."
She says she is not telling everyone they have to be a donor, but is encouraging people to "have those conversations" and register their preference on the organ donation registry so their loved ones know their wishes.
Anna-Louise has spoken to many children since and found they were "really open" to organ donation and more willing to discuss it than their adult parents, she says.
According to the NHS, some 408 people died last year while on the UK transplant waiting list, with Anna-Louise saying just 1% of people end up being eligible to be a donor.
Since 2015 in Wales, 2020 in England and 2021 in Scotland, authorities have operated an opt-out service, external, where adults are presumed to be donors unless they declare otherwise on the NHS Organ Donation Register.
But families will still be consulted and can object.
The system does not apply to people under 18 and decisions regarding children are made by their families, although anyone of any age can add themselves to the register.
Chloe in Middlesbrough is also asking people to think about it in advance, what would they do if the unthinkable happened?
"You do not want to think about your child dying, I understand that" she says.
"But look at the children doing well, what can come from thinking about it and making that decision to donate.
"I totally respect people's choices.
"It's just about thinking and talking about it."

title: Autonomisation des femmes de Dahra : le ministre Idrissa Samb remet des attestations de formation et des bons de financements à 306 femmes
content:
Autonomisation des femmes de Dahra : le ministre Idrissa Samb remet des attestations de formation et des bons de financements à 306 femmes
Le projet de formation professionnelle et d’insertion ( PFPI) mis en œuvre par Education Developement Center Senegal ( EDC Senegal ) avec l’appui technique et financier de la fondation Mastercard en partenariat avec la direction générale de la formation professionnelle et technique (DGFPT), la direction de l’insertion et la Direction de l’apprentissage du ministère de l’emploi et de la formation professionnelle et Technique a organisé ce vendredi une cérémonie de remise d’attestations de formation et de bons de financements au profit de 306 femmes de la commune de Dahra Djoloff dans le département de Linguère.
Cette cérémonie présidée par le ministre de la formation professionnelle et Technique Idrissa Samb s’inscrit dans le cadre des activités du PFPI, dont la poursuite du financement et de l’accompagnement des jeunes et des femmes à travers un fonds d’amorçage d’un montant de 863 millions de francs pour l’année 2026.
Au-delà de la remise symbolique des attestations et des bons de financement, cette rencontre est un moment de mobilisation de valorisation et d’engagement collectif en faveur de l’insertion socio-professionnelle et de l’autonomisation économique des femmes.
Il faut signaler que ces 306 femmes regroupées autour de neuf groupements qui reçoivent aujourd’hui leurs attestations de formation ont été auparavant initiées aux techniques de fabrication de savon, d’eau de javel, de transformations de fruits et légumes et des produits laitiers. Chaque regroupement féminin a reçu 750.000 FCFA pour un montant
Selon le ministre ces financements permettront à ces bonnes dames de créer, développer ou consolider leurs activités économiques et de renforcer leur autonomisation économique en favorisant leur accès à l’emploi et à l’entrepreneuriat. Il a par ailleurs demandé aux bénéficiaires d’utiliser à bon escient ce fonds.
Les bénéficiaires visiblement très satisfaits ont remercié l’état du Sénégal à travers le ministère de la formation professionnelle et technique pour leur avoir octroyé ces financements en vue de renforcer davantage leurs activités.

Trump is rolling back climate action. These 157 cities are going in the opposite direction
content: In June 2026, the Trump administration told states that they couldn’t use billions of dollars in Inflation Reduction Act federal rebates to help homeowners switch from fossil fuel appliances to climate-friendly heat pumps. But that move didn’t affect a heat pump rebate available in Tacoma, Washington, run by the city and its local power utility. It’s one example of how, even as the federal government takes a serious step back from climate action under the Trump administration, local leaders on the city and state level are still able to make climate progress with their own policies. A new database, from the University of Maryland’s Center for Global Sustainability, details such city-level actions. It covers more than 1,400 policies and programs from 157 cities across the country—from building efficiency upgrades to financial incentive programs to climate mitigation actions like increasing shade in cities affected by extreme heat. [Screenshot: University of Maryland] Called the U.S. City Climate & Energy Policy Database, the tool features both a map, which shows which cities have the most climate policies, and a dataset that links out to city plans and categorizes each action by location, sector, and policy area (such as transportation, electricity, or waste, for example). “This database gives us the clearest picture yet of how cities across the country are responding to the current moment with policy,” Nate Hultman, director of the Center for Global Sustainability at the University of Maryland, said in a statement. “What stands out is both the breadth of action and the opportunity it reveals: cities and states are pursuing clean energy and energy efficiency, and understanding that landscape is the first step toward accelerating action where it is needed most,” he added. Other examples of local climate action highlighted in the data set include Cleveland’s plan to overhaul city facilities with renewable energy and efficiency upgrades. The city has a climate plan, introduced in 2025, to cut emissions 63.3% by 2030, which would save residents $2.3 million in energy costs and create more than 1,200 jobs per year. In Phoenix—which saw its second-hottest summer on record this year—city officials are already in the process of adding shade to combat that heat. In 2024, the city launched a Shade Phoenix initiative to add 27,000 new trees and 550 new shade structures in the next five years. Not every policy in the database is recent; some date back a decade. But because they’re on the local level, they’re protected from the Trump administration’s efforts to tear down federal climate programs. We need city, state, and federal action on climate change. What this database shows, though, is that even when the federal government fails on this front, local governments can still take impactful actions. “The data show that local leadership is real, it is widespread, and it is providing the groundwork for a better pathway,” Hultman said.

title: Sudan’s Memory: Dr Khalid Farah Opens a New Window onto Darfur’s Social History
content:
Sudan’s Memory: Dr Khalid Farah Opens a New Window onto Darfur’s Social History
By Mohammed Al-Sheikh Hussein
Ambassador Dr Khalid Muhammad Farah’s book, Religious Education in Darfur in the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries AD, opens a new window onto Sudan’s social history.
(1)
If one thinks the book offers a new approach to writing the social history of the Sudanese people, that impression is entirely correct. It is the first scholarly book devoted to writing Sudanese social history.
And so that we do not arrive at the conclusions before considering the premises, it is useful to delve into the chapters of this book, which is the first scholarly work on the history of religious education in Darfur, focusing on the period of the Islamic Fur Sultanate during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries AD, which represented the height of the flourishing of religious education in the Darfur region.
(2)
In numerical terms, the book, published by Al-Musawwarat Publishing House, comprises 284 medium-format pages and consists of four chapters. It draws on a bibliography of 146 references, documents, manuscripts and oral interviews.
The book originated as a doctoral thesis in Sudanese Studies at the Mohammed Omer Bashir Centre for Sudanese Studies at Omdurman Ahlia University, under the supervision of Professor Mu’tasim Ahmed Al-Hajj.
(3)
The first chapter provides a historical introduction to Darfur and Islam, explaining how Islam entered Darfur from the sixteenth century AD through trade routes from North Africa and Chad. It also explains Darfur’s transformation into an officially Islamic sultanate under Sultan Suleiman Solong.
The chapter reviews the sultans’ role in supporting education, particularly through the construction of mosques and khalwas—traditional Qur’anic schools—and by bringing scholars to the region.
(4)
The second chapter examines the institutions of religious education in Darfur, explaining:
The khalwas, which constituted the fundamental nucleus of religious education, particularly in terms of the residential system, the relationship between the sheikh and the student, and the use of the wooden writing board (lawh) and inkpot (dawaya).
Mosques, where every congregational mosque hosted study circles in jurisprudence and tawhid (Islamic monotheism) after the prayers.
Sufi zawiyas, establishing that the people of Darfur were familiar with Sufism.
The role of the Tijaniyya and Sammaniyya Sufi orders in spreading the religious sciences.
The role of the sultan, and how rulers such as Muhammad Tayrab and Ali Dinar supported the khalwas and granted scholars land and exemptions.
(5)
The third chapter focuses on the curricula of study, setting out the educational programme followed during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
The first stage began with memorising the entire Qur’an according to the recitations of Warsh and Qalun.
In the second stage, students studied Maliki jurisprudential texts such as Al-Akhdari, Ibn Ashir and Al-Ashmawiyya.
In the third stage, they studied tawhid based on Al-Sanusi al-Sughra, the sciences of Hadith, the Prophetic biography, Arabic grammar and Alfiyyat Ibn Malik.
This was followed by a stage devoted to writing, including Arabic calligraphy, correspondence and legal documents.
(6)
The fourth chapter presents the most prominent scholars and khalwas during the period under study. The book lists the names of sheikhs and khalwas that became renowned, including the khalwas of Tawila, Kabkabiya and Al-Fashir.
Among the scholars from the Dinar family, the most prominent was Sultan Ahmed Dinar.
The book provides extensive accounts of scholars from Morocco, Egypt, and Chad who settled in Darfur. It also examines the system of ijazah, the scholarly authorisation a sheikh grants to a student.
(7)
The fourth chapter also addresses the role of religious education in society.
This is the most important chapter in the book for the following reasons:
It highlights the social role of the sheikh, who simultaneously served as a judge, mediator and teacher.
It examines the sheikh’s political role as an adviser to the sultans, as well as his work as a writer and official in the administrative bureaus.
It examines the economic role of the khalwas, which functioned as centres of production, as students engaged in agriculture and livestock herding in order to support themselves.
It demonstrates the central role of religious education in unifying society. It was a common factor shared by the Arab and Zurqa communities.
(8)
The book also examines the challenges posed by external invasion from several perspectives, most notably:
The impact of the Egyptian invasion of 1874 on the khalwas.
How Darfur preserved the independence of its educational curricula despite external pressures.
The book concludes that religious education in Darfur during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries constituted an integrated system rather than merely an exercise in memorisation or rote instruction. It produced judges, imams, scribes and administrators who governed the sultanate for 300 years.
(9)
The importance of this book lies in the following points:
It provides scholarly documentation, drawing on manuscripts, documents, and interviews with khalwa sheikhs.
It demonstrates that Darfur experienced a scholarly renaissance before the emergence of formal, modern schools.
It serves as a reference for researchers studying Sudan’s history of education.

title: From wanting to be seen as white to finding his way back to te reo Māori
content:
Ake, Ake, Ake - A forever language
Nathan Grey (Ngāti Porou, Ngāti Tūwharetoa, Ngāti Raukawa) grew up knowing he was Māori but not knowing much about what that meant.
His grandparents belonged to a generation where te reo Māori had been suppressed, and he was taught that success meant moving away from his Māoritanga, his identity.
"I didn't grow up with te reo. I didn't know anything and I didn't actually want to know anything," he said.
"I was always told that to be successful you had to be white.
"So I made that my mission to surround myself with Pākehā... in high school I was white.
"I was called the Dalmatian and I was proud of that. I was like, yo, that means it's working. Like I am brown, but actually people see me as white."
His older brother would eventually give him a different way of seeing himself.
After his brother completed a full-immersion te reo Māori course at Te Wānanga Takiura, Grey felt a pull to reclaim his ancestral language.
Grey enrolled at the same wānanga and began a journey that would eventually lead him to teaching te reo Māori himself.
Looking back, he said he had always known he would return to a part of himself that had been missing.
"You sort of know somewhere that you end up returning to the place of which has been missing from you for a while," he said.
"And because of suppressing the person who I was in high school, that was bound to come up eventually after that. So I like to think it naturally happened."
But reconnecting with that part of himself was not easy. Grey said learning te reo brought up feelings of mamae he had spent years pushing away.
"Honestly, it was like one of the hardest things.
"Because for 20 years I just put these feelings away and then having to get into a space where you have to face that... You're like, whoa, what is happening?"
He described the experience as scary but said Takiura taught him to lean on the people around him.
"They're all doing the same thing. They're all going through that same feeling as well," he said.
"And you just talk about it and you just come to understand like, oh my God, like yeah, this isn't the fault of ours.
"We shouldn't have to feel ashamed or embarrassed about the feelings, about us not knowing what we should know."
Now a kaiako of te reo Māori at Selwyn Community Education, Grey said learning te reo Māori has only opened more doors.
"It sort of got me into spaces like this [teaching], got me into spaces working with people, like social work and things like that.
"So very grateful that I've been able to actually learn about who I am. Because it's not like just the language, it's about you and then whatever follows that as well."
His ākonga all come from many different backgrounds, including fifth generation Pākehā and tauiwi learners from countries such as Argentina.
Many tell him they want to learn because they want to respect and better understand the country they live in.
Grey said he loves seeing people from different backgrounds come together through te reo Māori.
"I think it's super important for the reo to be shared in a way that is mindful of what you're sharing, but also not trying to make it a scary experience for those who are wanting to embark on it, but are a little bit whakamā," he said.
"They don't know how to approach it, but they want to approach it in a respectful way."
He said the more people who learn te reo Māori, the more understanding there can be of Māori culture and people.
"I just think the more people who speak te reo, the better," he said.
"The better the country, the more understanding we have to the culture and the people.
"Things that are good for Māori are good for everyone."
Grey hopes his students leave knowing they are capable of learning the language, even if they feel whakamā at first.
"I hope that they take away that they can actually do it, that they have the ability to do so, and then there's people around them to tautoko them for that," he said.
"And you can see the keenness that they have for it. So I just hope they hold on to that keenness and carry on, really, with their mahi."

title: Anti-bullying tribunal receives 55 complaints, 5 settled
content:
Five of the cases were decided through various awards, including bullies being made to apologise to their victims, undergo counselling or, in one case, pay RM2,000 in damages, she said.
“These measures show that the tribunal is punishment-oriented but also focusses on rehabilitation of victims and the perpetrators’ behaviour,” she said in a statement.
Azalina said the Anti-Bullying Act 2026 and the tribunal provided a specific mechanism for dealing with bullying through a restorative approach that was faster and more cost-effective, while placing greater emphasis on protecting and rehabilitating victims.
However, she said, laws alone would not be enough to tackle bullying.
“The victims must come forward to seek help, while those who witness bullying must have the courage to speak up because bullying is not a joke and must not be normalised under any circumstances,” she said.
The tribunal serves as a second avenue for victims who believe their complaints are not properly addressed by educational institutions.
It also handles cases involving children outside the school system.

title: Oncology Care Model-Related Increases in Screening for Depression and Pain and Patient-Reported Symptoms.
content: Many patients with cancer experience pain or depression. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services' Oncology Care Model (OCM) included practice-reported quality measures aiming to improve screening and management of pain and depression. We described changes over time and assessed concurrent changes in patient-reported symptoms over time. We studied patients receiving chemotherapy at OCM-participating practices. We evaluated practice-reported information about screening and management of pain and depression and patient experience survey data collected quarterly during 2017-2022. We assessed changes in practice-reported rates of screening and management of pain and depression. We also estimated time trends in patient-reported symptoms of pain and emotional problems, such as anxiety and depression, as well as receipt of help for these problems, using a spline function at the start of the COVID-19 public health emergency, adjusting for patient and practice characteristics. Practice-reported rates of pain screening and management improved from 76.5% to 92.6% from 2017 to 2022; depression screening and management rates improved from 56.6% to 81.7%. Concurrent assessments of patient-reported pain (-0.2 percentage points (pp)/quarter; P = .002) and emotional problems (-0.1 pp/quarter; P = .001) decreased slightly pre-COVID; trends for both symptoms were stable during COVID-19 (P > .20). Among patients reporting pain or emotional problems, there were slight decreases in reports of receiving help with these symptoms from their cancer care team before and during COVID-19 (all P < .06). Despite substantial practice-reported increases in screening for pain and depression, concurrently collected measures of patient-reported pain and emotional problems declined very slightly and patient reports of receiving help from their cancer care team for these symptoms did not improve. Strategies beyond screening may be needed to better address pain and depression among patients receiving cancer treatment.

title: Timely emergency care saves Chinese passenger from critical condition
content:
QUẢNG NINH — A Chinese passenger who had fainted and lost consciousness has been provided first aid by the Móng Cái International Border Guard Station, helping him through a critical episode.
At around 2pm on Friday, while processing passengers at the immigration counter at the Móng Cái International Border Gate, the officers noticed Liang Ruizhuang, 67, Chinese nationality, suddenly faint, lose consciousness and become unable to stand unaided.
Immediately upon noticing the incident, Lieutenant Colonel Dương Đại Thắng and Lieutenant Colonel Hoàng Trung Thanh quickly approached, administered first aid and carried out an initial check on the male passenger.
Observing that Liang Ruizhuang was weak and foaming at the mouth, the officers urgently contacted and coordinated with the international health quarantine force to examine and check his health, and to continue monitoring his condition.
Thanks to the prompt detection, assistance and intervention, after about 30 minutes Liang Ruizhuang recovered and regained consciousness.
Afterwards, the male passenger was taken to the Móng Cái Regional General Hospital for further treatment. — VNS

title: New Vocational GCSEs unveiled in major shake-up to hands-on learning for teens
content:
New Vocational GCSEs unveiled in major shake-up to hands-on learning for teens
New Vocational GCSEs for students to study vocational courses at school, with nationally-set content, grading and assessment, alongside a strong academic core of English, maths and science,
Every young person across the country will be able to pursue prestigious new Vocational GCSEs and access work experience in a major shake-up of the education system to prepare them for the world of work.
Delivering on the Prime Minister’s commitment in his first week in the role to put technical education on an equal footing with the traditional academic path, the new national qualifications will be created to sit alongside traditional GCSEs and will replace the current Technical Awards.
Part of action to revolutionise technical and vocational learning, the rigorous new qualifications will help ensure today’s students have the skills for the jobs of the future.
The shake-up builds on reforms including new V Levels, Occupational and Foundational Certificates and expanded T Levels – giving young people more routes to a brighter future, ensuring they have a clear line of sight to employment, and helping to tackle the crisis of the 1 million young people who are out of education, employment or training.
Alongside revolutions inside the classroom, the government is launching a National Mission on Work Experience, working alongside the Good Growth Business Forum and other businesses, to boost opportunities outside the classroom.
It is a call to arms to employers to provide an additional 200,000 work experience placements to ensure all young people have vital exposure to the workplace between 14 and 16, with Mayors and local authorities helping to make links between schools and employers. This could include spending time in key sectors including accountancy firms, digital media companies and construction companies. Employers can contact their local Careers Hub to pledge new work experience placements.
Alongside businesses, No10 North will establish work experience placements for 14-16 year old students this academic year. This will give young people the chance to see into the heart of government, experience the world of work, and demonstrate the real opportunities available to them on their doorstep
It is part of the Prime Minister’s mission to fix the most difficult issues facing the country, and create opportunities in every postcode.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:
We’ve all heard someone say ‘school wasn’t really for me’ because they were not given the chance to study vocational courses as well as traditional subjects.
That one-size-fits-all approach isn’t working, so we’re building an education system that values both academic and technical paths.
I want to give all young people across Britain the hope that their future will be brighter - whether it starts at university or not.
Education Secretary Lucy Powell said:
Young people today are entering a world of work full of exciting opportunities. We need to prepare them for it. Time and again young people, parents and employers tell me they want schools to do more to help them understand and prepare for the jobs of the future.
That is why we are transforming technical education and ensuring every young person can access the knowledge, skills and experiences they need to thrive in a changing world.
Our new Vocational GCSEs will give young people a stronger connection to the careers and industries shaping our economy, helping them discover and develop their talents while maintaining high standards across our education system.
This is not about creating different routes for different children. It is about ensuring every child has access to a rich and ambitious education that opens doors, creates opportunity and prepares them for life beyond the classroom.
The same size as GCSEs, these new qualifications will be nationally set, with subject content based on subject expert advice. Assessment and grading will be regulated by Ofqual to ensure full parity with traditional GCSEs.
They will eventually replace existing Technical Awards, which currently vary by provider with no nationally set content, and do not consistently support progression to further study.
They are set to be available in some subjects from as early as September 2029, as part of broader new technical pathways starting in September 2028. Subject options could include Business Management and Finance, Creative Media Production, Digital Tech, Child Development, and Building and Construction, supporting progression into further study through T Levels and V Levels in these subjects, or through A Levels.
New subjects will be developed as part of a review of existing GCSEs and new Vocational GCSEs, to create a complementary set of qualifications that give students greater choice, but avoid duplication or unnecessary overlap. English, Maths and Science will remain a common entitlement. Together, the qualifications on offer at age 14 will be aligned to 16-19 progression routes including A Levels, T Levels and the new V Levels.
The work to move away from a one-size-fits-all system designed in Whitehall was kicked off earlier this month as the Education Secretary hosted a summit at No10 North with mayors, businesses, schools and colleges.
Sir Hamid Patel CBE, Chief Executive of Star Academies, said:
Over the past two decades, we have strengthened GCSEs through greater rigour, clearer and more coherently sequenced subject content, and more robust assessment. These reforms extend those same high standards into vocational education, ensuring qualifications are underpinned by nationally agreed content, strong regulatory oversight and clear progression routes into apprenticeships, T Levels, V Levels, A Levels, higher education and employment.
The new vocational GCSEs have the potential to command the confidence of parents, employers, colleges and universities alike, while providing young people with meaningful pathways into high-skilled careers. Importantly, they will sit alongside a strong core academic education, ensuring that pupils continue to study the essential subjects that underpin future success. Crucially, they can help ensure that education is better aligned to the skills and workforce needs of local communities and regional economies, supporting the growth ambitions of mayors and combined authorities across the country.
John Yarham, Chief Executive Officer, The Careers & Enterprise Company, said:
We welcome the national mission on work experience. High-quality pathways, alongside modern work experience, are vital to bringing the world of work to life and giving young people the skills and knowledge they need for their future.
Employers of all sizes and sectors tell us they see real benefits from outreach that builds diverse future talent. To make this happen at scale, we need an ambitious shared framework, underpinned by strong local coordination, so opportunities are targeted where they can have the greatest impact – particularly for young people currently missing out.
CEC stands ready to work with our Careers Hub partners in every region, connecting employers with schools and colleges to create more high-quality opportunities and bridge the gap between education and the world of work.
Michelle Ovens CBE, CEO & Founder of Small Business Britain, said:
We’re pleased to see the government’s mission to boost work experience opportunities for young people. Small businesses across the country are often where young people get their first exposure to the world of work, helping them build practical skills and experience, while also playing a vital role in strengthening local and regional economies.
Stronger public-private partnerships between government, education and business are vital to ensuring young people leave education with the skills, experience, and confidence they need to navigate the world of work, and that small businesses are equipped to help provide those opportunities.
Sarah Bradbury, Chief Executive of IGD, said:
Modern work experience has the power to open young people’s eyes to careers they may never have considered and give them the skills and confidence to take that first step into work. Through our industry-wide Feeding Britain’s Future movement, businesses within the food and drink industry are trialling a new, flexible approach in partnership with The Careers & Enterprise Company, that brings employers together to create meaningful work experiences at scale. The food and drink industry is the UK’s largest private sector employer and we want young people to see the huge range of opportunities it offers. We welcome the national mission on work experience and stand ready to work with industry to bridge the gap between schools, colleges and the world of work.
Shevaun Haviland CBE, Director General of the British Chambers of Commerce said:
Business leaders are deeply committed to their communities and want to support young people on their journey from education to employment.
That’s why the British Chambers of Commerce is pleased to support the National Mission on Work Experience, and will work through our Chambers, who are already closely engaged with both businesses and schools across the country, to rally local employers to the cause.
Expanding access to work experience and increased business engagement in schools is critical to supporting the workforce of tomorrow. It is welcome that this government initiative is being delivered in partnership with business organisations.
Irene Graham, CEO, ScaleUp Institute, said:
Scaling firms, across sectors and regions, are strong supporters of work experience. This National Mission is a vital one to help young people’s entry in to the world of the work and the ScaleUp Institute looks forward to supporting the initiative as it develops.
Rt Hon Robert Halfon, Executive Director of Made UK said:
Manufacturers and Make UK warmly welcome the National Mission on Work Experience and the Government’s commitment to expanding technical education. The Prime Minister is right that the gap between the classroom and the workplace has to be bridged if we are to equip young people with the skills employers need.
For too long, too many young people have left school without meaningful exposure to the world of work or a clear understanding of the opportunities available to them. Work experience and technical education can be transformative, helping young people develop confidence, build employability skills and gain the knowledge and practical experience that employers value.
This call on employers across the country to create more opportunities is an important step forward, but what matters now is quality. Delivering the right mix of technical knowledge and practical application, backed by qualifications employers recognise and close collaboration between industry and education, will ensure every young person has the chance to access a genuine ladder of opportunity into skilled, well-paid careers.
Rob Nitsch CEO Federation of Awarding Bodies said;
These developments are positive; it is absolutely right that the blend of classroom and practical learning should be extended, and that the focus is on better choices at 16. Awarding Organisations will also welcome the acknowledgement of the place of practical skills assessments in courses of learning that are practical in nature and will look forward to contributing to the development of the new pathways.
Alan Milburn’s interim report into NEETs commissioned by the government warned that Britain is at risk of a “lost generation”. His findings painted a stark picture of a system that too often leaves young people leaving school without the skills, experience or connections they need to step into the world of work.
He pointed to “strong evidence” that practical learning is effective in helping those at risk of being NEET move into work.
The White Working Class Inquiry also laid bare the lack of opportunity for working-class children to thrive, concluding that the technical and vocational system is broken for disadvantaged groups.
It highlighted that vocational and technical routes are valued highly by white working-class families, and recommend a major structural overhaul of technical and vocational routes to help close the disadvantage gap.
Notes to Editors
- Local leaders, employers, schools and colleges will play a key role in deciding the subjects to reflect skills needs. A consultation will also be launched later in the year to help shape the new qualifications and get views from local leaders.
- It comes on top of ambitious curriculum and GCSE reforms that will make sure schools are preparing youngsters to have the knowledge and skills needed to genuinely thrive in the workplace. As part of this, there will be a greater emphasis on practical skills and assessments in practical GCSE subjects such as PE, Drama, Design and Technology, Food and Nutrition, Music and Computing to properly recognise the value of these skills and further support students to succeed beyond the classroom.
- The government will adapt school performance measures ensuring Ofsted and the accountability system support these new qualifications, so schools are appropriately incentivised to offer these valuable opportunities for young people.
- 16 year olds will be able to take the first V Levels in Education, Finance and Digital, from September 2027, alongside new T Levels in Sports, Fitness and Exercise Science, and Care Services from 2028. New Occupational and Further Study Pathways are also being introduced to help students progress onto A, V or T Levels, or into employment or an apprenticeship.
- Work experience for 14 to 16 year olds is additional to the industry placements that students currently complete through T Levels.
- Members of the Good Growth Business Forum include:
- British Chambers of Commerce
- Citizens Advice
- Co-operatives UK
- Confederation of British Industry
- Enterprise Nation
- Family Business UK
- Federation of Small Businesses
- Institute of Directors
- Make UK
- ScaleUp Institute
- Small Business Britain
- Social Enterprise UK
- Staffline Recruitment
- Startup Coalition
- Trades Union Congress

title: IN PICS | ‘He died for what he believed in’: Stars pay tribute at Owen Ndlovu memorial
content:
Story audio is generated using AI
Family members, close friends and industry figures, including Ntsiki Mazwai, Vusi Leeuw, Tebogo Sithathu and Mercy Pakela, gathered at the Walter Sisulu Hall in Randburg on Wednesday to pay their respects at the memorial service for broadcaster and music rights activist Owen Ndlovu.
Ndlovu died aged 54 on September 16. According to police reports, his body was discovered on the side of a road in Thokoza the morning after he was kidnapped outside a Katlehong church while picking up his wife.
Tributes poured in throughout the service with speeches remembering Ndlovu as a brave, relentless man with passion and an unwavering commitment to artists’ economic rights.
Recalling a friendship spanning more than 30 years since they first met at JoziFM, music and talent consultant Leeuw described Ndlovu as a pioneer who was among the first generation of community radio broadcasters.
“Out of everything we knew about Owen, this situation was the last one I would ever think of, that he would leave this earth like that,” he said.
“Owen was a pioneer because he was one of the first generation of community radio broadcasters in South Africa.”
Leeuw said one of the messages Ndlovu left his wife with before he died was that he and performing artist Eugene Mthethwa should be united to assist the industry where it needs to go.
When Mthethwa stepped on stage, he burst into tears and shared the same sentiments.
“He was fighting, not for his own rights but for composers. He was selfless. Owen died for commitment. Owen used his resources to fight the battles,” Mthethwa said.
The EFF MP and Trompies member said he had opened the bag Ndlovu’s body was found with and said it was filled with Southern African Music Rights Organisation (Samro) documents.
“He took Samro to court. Owen was very meticulous. He won the case against the CEO of Samro who was barring him from entering the (Samro) building.
“We have the bag. In Owen’s death, we multiply. It is for us to continue the battle. We must reclaim our rights. We can’t be begging people for our rights. He died for what he believed in.”
Ahead of Ndlovu’s burial on Friday, Mthethwa said he made every effort to ensure he is buried at Heroes’ Acre in Pretoria where renowned public figures have been laid to rest.
“I fought for him to be buried at Heroes’ Acre because he deserves it. He was not a coward.”
Actress and arts activist Joy Mbewana said: “Owen was taken away from us. He was a man willing to risk all for the truth. The fight does not end here.”
Veteran pop singer Mercy Pakela described Ndlovu as a saviour when recounting how he secured a pro-bono lawyer for her to fight Samro for her unpaid royalties at for music dating back to 1990.
“I still cannot believe it. It’s very hard for me to believe. He’s a fighter. Wherever he is in the spiritual realm, he’s fighting for us. All he did was to fight for artists’ economic rights and livelihoods. We will never stop There’s no-one who’s done that. Owen did it for us. Today we know we have an ancestor in the spirit fighting for us,” she said.
“Artists die as paupers, but officials drive fancy cars and have beautiful homes. Artists suffer the consequences and Owen was fighting that, exposing the corruption and the rot at Samro. He had money, he was wealthy — it’s not that he wanted to make money out of artists.”
The memorial service coincided with a poignant personal moment, falling on the birthday of Ndlovu’s son Owethu. When he took to the stage alongside his brothers, he spoke about how much he had learned from his father.
“I never understood why you were so hard on me, but now I understand,” he said.

title: ΑΑΔΕ: 30 απαντήσεις στα συχνότερα προβλήματα κατά την υποβολή της Ενιαίας Αίτησης Ενίσχυσης 2026
content:
ΑΑΔΕ: 30 απαντήσεις στα συχνότερα προβλήματα κατά την υποβολή της Ενιαίας Αίτησης Ενίσχυσης 2026


ΑΑΔΕ: 30 απαντήσεις στα συχνότερα προβλήματα κατά την υποβολή της Ενιαίας Αίτησης Ενίσχυσης 2026
Οι διευκρινίσεις αφορούν, μεταξύ άλλων, τα ηλεκτρονικά μισθωτήρια, τα ιδιοκτησιακά ζητήματα και τη δήλωση αγροτεμαχίων, τα κτηνοτροφικά στοιχεία, τα αιτήματα για αγροτικές ενισχύσεις, τη διασύνδεση του myAGRO με το myDATA
Απαντήσεις σε 30 συχνά ερωτήματα, που έχουν τεθεί από παραγωγούς και φορείς υποβολής αιτήσεων για την Ενιαία Αίτηση Ενίσχυσης (ΕΑΕ) 2026, έδωσε η Ανεξάρτητη Αρχή Δημοσίων Εσόδων (ΑΑΔΕ), στο πλαίσιο της συνεχούς ενημέρωσης για την πορεία των παρεμβάσεων και της λειτουργίας της πλατφόρμας myAGRO.

Οι διευκρινίσεις αφορούν, μεταξύ άλλων, τα ηλεκτρονικά μισθωτήρια, τα ιδιοκτησιακά ζητήματα και τη δήλωση αγροτεμαχίων, τα κτηνοτροφικά στοιχεία, τα αιτήματα για αγροτικές ενισχύσεις, τη διασύνδεση του myAGRO με το myDATA και άλλες εφαρμογές της ΑΑΔΕ, καθώς και ειδικότερα τεχνικά θέματα σχετικά με τους αριθμούς ΑΤΑΚ και ΚΑΕΚ.

Όπως σημειώνει η Ανεξάρτητη Αρχή σε μισθώσεις με περισσότερους από έναν εκμισθωτές δεν απαιτείται τροποποίηση ή εκ νέου σύναψη μισθωτηρίου, ούτε προκύπτει πρόστιμο για τον λόγο αυτό. Τα ηλεκτρονικά μισθωτήρια εμφανίζονται στο myAGRO εφόσον έχουν καταχωρηθεί στη σχετική δήλωση της ΑΑΔΕ και δεν έχουν απορριφθεί, ενώ σε περίπτωση που κάποιο μισθωτήριο δεν εμφανίζεται, παρέχεται δυνατότητα χειροκίνητης καταχώρισης, ώστε να μην καθυστερεί η υποβολή. Παράλληλα, επιβεβαιώνεται ότι είναι δυνατή χωρίς πρόστιμο η ηλεκτρονική καταχώριση παλαιών έγχαρτων μισθωτηρίων.

Σε ό,τι αφορά τα ιδιοκτησιακά, δίνει ειδικές οδηγίες για τις περιπτώσεις εκκρεμούς κληρονομικής διαδοχής. Όταν ο ιδιοκτήτης έχει αποβιώσει από την 1η Ιανουαρίου 2026 και μετά, ο κληρονόμος μπορεί, υπό τις προβλεπόμενες προϋποθέσεις, να υποβάλει την ΕΑΕ 2026 στον ΑΦΜ του θανόντος. Για μισθωμένα αγροτεμάχια, η υφιστάμενη μίσθωση θεωρείται ότι παραμένει σε ισχύ και ο μισθωτής μπορεί να επιλέξει ως λόγο μη επιβεβαίωσης του ΑΤΑΚ την ένδειξη «Κληρονομιά». Αντίθετα, για θανάτους έως και 31 Δεκεμβρίου 2025 απαιτείται νέο μισθωτήριο με τους κληρονόμους.

Διευκρινίσεις παρέχονται, επίσης, για αγροτεμάχια με δασικό χαρακτηρισμό που στο Κτηματολόγιο εμφανίζονται ως «Δημόσιες Γαίες», καθώς και για την αντιστοίχιση ΑΤΑΚ και ΚΑΕΚ. Η ΑΑΔΕ επισημαίνει ότι δεν υπάρχει γενικός αποκλεισμός των δασικών εκτάσεων, ενώ σε συγκεκριμένες περιπτώσεις ο παραγωγός πρέπει να δηλώσει τον λόγο χρήσης του σχετικού ΚΑΕΚ. Για ιδιοχρησιμοποιούμενα αγροτεμάχια ισχύει ο κανόνας αντιστοίχισης ενός ΑΤΑΚ με έναν ΚΑΕΚ, με τις σχετικές διορθώσεις στο Ε9 να μην επιφέρουν πρόστιμο.

Στα αιτήματα ενισχύσεων, η ΑΑΔΕ υπογραμμίζει ότι έχει επιλυθεί το ζήτημα καταχώρισης της συνδεδεμένης ενίσχυσης για τη σόγια. Παράλληλα, διευκρινίζεται ότι για την ενίσχυση γεωργών νεαρής ηλικίας μπορούν να υποβάλλουν αίτημα γεωργοί έως 40 ετών, ενώ δικαίωμα διατηρούν και όσοι είχαν κριθεί δικαιούχοι από το 2022 και μετά και πλέον έχουν υπερβεί το συγκεκριμένο ηλικιακό όριο.

Τέλος, σε σχέση με τη διασύνδεση των συστημάτων, η ΑΑΔΕ σημειώνει ότι το myAGRO αντλεί τα παραστατικά που έχουν καταχωρηθεί στο myDATA, ενώ οι νέες καταχωρίσεις ενημερώνουν την πλατφόρμα εντός χρονικού διαστήματος έως δύο ωρών.

Ερώτημα 1. Σε μισθώσεις με περισσότερους από έναν εκμισθωτές, το κοινό μισθωτήριο αναγνωρίζει μόνο έναν ιδιοκτήτη. Απαιτείται σύναψη νέου μισθωτηρίου με καταβολή προστίμου;

Στην εφαρμογή myAGRO αντλούνται όλα τα στοιχεία των μισθώσεων από τις Δηλώσεις Πληροφοριακών Στοιχείων Μίσθωσης (ΔΠΣΜ) της ΑΑΔΕ. Τα στοιχεία αυτά περιλαμβάνουν όλους τους εκμισθωτές που έχουν δηλωθεί.
Στην περίπτωση που δεν έχει δηλωθεί κανένας ΑΤΑΚ στην ΔΠΣΜ, ο παραγωγός πρέπει να καταχωρήσει τουλάχιστον έναν ΑΤΑΚ στην εφαρμογή myAGRO. Η καταχώρηση ΑΤΑΚ των λοιπών συνεκμισθωτών είναι προαιρετική.
Συνεπώς δεν απαιτείται τροποποίηση ή εκ νέου σύναψη του μισθωτηρίου και δεν προκύπτει υποχρέωση καταβολής προστίμου για το λόγο αυτόν.

Όχι. Στο myAGRO εμφανίζονται τα ηλεκτρονικά μισθωτήρια που έχουν καταχωρηθεί στη ΔΠΣΜ της ΑΑΔΕ για τα οποία δεν έχει δηλωθεί απόρριψη, ανεξαρτήτως δηλαδή εάν έχει πραγματοποιηθεί ρητή αποδοχή ή όχι.

Απαντήσεις σε συχνά ερωτήματα
Οι απαντήσεις καλύπτουν τα ηλεκτρονικά μισθωτήρια, τα ζητήματα ψηφιοποίησης και δήλωσης των αγροτεμαχίων, τα κτηνοτροφικά στοιχεία, τα αιτήματα ενισχύσεων, τη διασύνδεση με τις λοιπές εφαρμογές της Αρχής και επιμέρους τεχνικά θέματα.A. Μισθωτήρια που είναι δηλωμένα στην ΑΑΔΕ
Ερώτημα 1. Σε μισθώσεις με περισσότερους από έναν εκμισθωτές, το κοινό μισθωτήριο αναγνωρίζει μόνο έναν ιδιοκτήτη. Απαιτείται σύναψη νέου μισθωτηρίου με καταβολή προστίμου;
