Join todayAlready a member? Log in
Two men who were wrongfully arrested by a corrupt police officer have had theft convictions quashed after 50 years.
Christopher Poulter and Kevin Biggs were 21 and 18 respectively when they were convicted in 1976 of taking 13 mailbags from a wagon in Clapham goods yard in London.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) referred their case to the Court of Appeal earlier this year after new evidence about disgraced police officer Detective Sergeant Derek Ridgewell.
Ridgewell was jailed for seven years in 1980 after stealing more than £1 million in goods and was found to have framed innocent young black men for his own crimes, the CCRC said.
He was one of three officers said to have seen Mr Poulter and Mr Biggs taking the mailbags and fleeing by car.
The men’s defence was that they had been in a pub in Tooting, south London, all night, before being approached by officers and arrested.
At Inner London Crown Court, Mr Poulter was given a year in prison and Mr Biggs was sentenced to borstal training.
The innocence of Mr Biggs, who died in 2004, emerged through an investigation by the British Transport Police, who were searching for victims of Ridgewell.
He and Mr Poulter are the 14th and 15th people to have their convictions quashed in relation to Ridgewell’s misconduct.
They were convicted alongside a third man, Stephen Simmons, whose conviction was quashed in 2018.
At a hearing on Tuesday, Lord Justice Edis, sitting with Mr Justice Lavender and Mr Justice Linden, said their appeals should have been heard together.
He said: “It had not been possible to add any relatives of Mr Biggs, who had by then died, or find Mr Poulter, so they could be joined on to the appeal by Mr Simmons.”
He added: “The two appeals are allowed and the convictions quashed.”
Speaking after the hearing, Jenny Wiltshire, head of serious and general crime at Hickman and Rose and who has represented many of Ridgewell’s victims, said it was a “disgrace” that British Transport Police had taken so long to track people down.
She said: “It is now half a century since these two men were found guilty of a crime they did not commit.
“The British Transport Police knew for certain that the police officer whose evidence sent them to jail was corrupt just four years after they were convicted, and probably a lot earlier.
“The British Transport Police did nothing at the time; and have only relatively recently started to take this issue seriously.
“As a result of this inaction, Christopher Poulter has lived the majority of his life as a convicted criminal. Kevin Biggs died as one.”
A spokesperson from the British Transport Police previously said: “The corrupt actions of former DS Ridgewell were first brought to our attention in 2020 following the overturning of convictions, and our dedicated team continue to review historic investigations and convictions to establish whether there are any further potential victims of corruption.”
CCRC chairwoman Dame Vera Baird KC said: “It is absolutely right that these men have had their convictions quashed by the court today.
“Anyone else who believes they have been convicted through the actions of Derek Ridgewell should apply to us so we can investigate whether we can also refer your case to the courts.”

title: PERCY MABANDU | A large sense of our heritage
content:
There is a photograph that challenges our often neutered and depoliticised meaning of heritage. Stretching our taste for Dutch wax dresses and braaied meat to mementos and memories of the sacrifices that shaped our struggle for human rights and liberation.
It belongs to the late great Drum generation photojournalist Anjith Kally and it is part of the “Homecoming” exhibition of the Johannesburg Art Gallery (JAG) collection. It’s currently on show downtown at the Standard Bank Art Gallery.
In the picture, Kally gives us the image of the late ANC president, Oliver Tambo, walking among open coffins at a mass funeral of 42 people killed by the South African Defence Force (SADF) during a midnight cross-border raid into Maseru, Lesotho, on December 9, 1982. Among the dead were 30 South Africans political refugees, mostly ANC members, and 12 Basotho nationals. Tambo is among the crowds who have gathered to pay their last respects to the dead.
Seen from the safe distance of more than three decades of democracy, Kally’s photograph should move us to expand our meaning of heritage. We should ask ourselves: what are the values and stories that we inherit, and who are the heroes and myths we reach for when the headwinds are roughest?
These questions matter because the heart of any culture is to be found in the nature of its hero. Who is that man or woman who is revered? Is it the prophet and the witchdoctor, the warrior and the liberator, or is it the glamorous politician and the thief?
At a time when media reports were littered with characterisations of freedom fighters as terrorists, Kally chose to reveal the freedom fighter as a man of gentler concerns for the brutalised people. He does not present us with a picture of a guerrilla at a podium. He catches Tambo mid-gait of a heavy-hearted walk at the head of gaping coffins. The leader is visibly tender, and rests his fisted right hand on his chest. Nursing unspoken hurts.
This conflation of the grand political moment with Tambo’s fleeting moment of vulnerability lends poignancy to the pictured moment.
Kally’s picture makes two important points: it acknowledges the frailty of the oppressed. Importantly, he also announces that the people will not be diminished or made less, and brevity of their lives because their death nourishes a heritage of struggles for freedom and human rights everywhere.
Enjoyed and mediated through the grainy black-and-white aesthetic in an art gallery, the image of open coffins at Tambo’s feet can feel too historical to be real; too distant, and rendered academic by time and Kally’s camera. However, that is part of the gift. The absence of fear and anxiety about potential harassment from the state.
The exhibition has other heirlooms of our struggle for dignity and human rights. Notable among these is a portrait of Dr Fabian Ribeiro by Andrew Motjuwadi. Before his premature death in 1968, Motjuwadi spent most of his life working and living in Mamelodi, where Dr Ribeiro and his wife Florence Barbara Ribeiro were gunned down in their courtyard by apartheid policemen. The state accused them of providing free medical care to injured activists and providing funds to young people who wanted to go and join the liberation armies outside the country. Their killers were granted amnesty in 1999 at the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
Motjuwadi’s portrait of Dr Ribeiro is a masterwork of balance; an amalgam of riotous texture and colour depicting his pensive profile. The picture portrays a seated, bespectacled Dr Ribeiro as he peers at what could be a medical document or a letter from a comrade. Motjuwadi has read well the idiosyncratic sober serenity that can be gleaned in almost all of the surviving photographs of the martyred doctor. This is a testament of both the artist’s observational skill, as well as the enduring qualities of his subjects personality.
Part of what gives these collected artworks an enduring meaning as treasures of our shared heritage is reading them alongside the works of other less politically-charged masterpieces from Europe and elsewhere. This exhibition includes works by titans of the Western canon like Paul Cézanne and Pablo Picasso, Vincent Van Gogh and Claude Monet; their work is seen alongside great South African painters like Maggie Laubser and Irma Stern, along with Gladys Mgudlandlu and George Pemba.
The global character of the variety of the masterworks on show speaks to the ambitions that informed how the JAGs collection was made. The examples of European modernism in the collection was meant to make a statement about the city of Johannesburg as as a beacon of modernity on the African subcontinent. As it grew, the collection now includes works by native artists to given a more democratically rooted vision of the city and its people.
The global character of the variety of the masterworks on show speaks to the ambitions that informed how the JAGs collection was made.
The exhibition is a result of a partnership between the City of Johannesburg and Standard Bank to bring a significant portion of the JAG’s prized collection back into public view while the gallery undergoes refurbishment.
It has been co-curated by Khwezi Gule, chief curator at the JAG, and Dr Same Mdluli, Standard Bank curator and gallery manager, with assistance from Bamanye Ngale and Gcotyelwa Mashiqa. They say their effort aims to reframe these historic works of art within a contemporary civic context.
Their publicity materials also state that this public-private partnership aims to anchor art as part of the heritage that encourages residents to re-enter the city and encounter its layered histories anew.
As the chatter of this heritage month heats our path to the polls in November, may it also enlarge our sense of the meaning of heritage.
The lofty traditions we accrued on our historic struggle for freedom and democracy in the world should be at the heart of it. Many lives were spent to mount a bulwark against tyranny and despair. We should bolster and cherish it with equal fervour.
“Homecoming” is set to run until October 31. We should all make time to go to see it.
- Mabandu is a writer and art historian. He lives in the City of Tshwane.

title: Δίπλα στο Αρκαλοχώρι για μια ακόμα χρονιά η ΠΑΕ Ολυμπιακός (pic)
content:
Ο Ολυμπιακός και ο Βαγγέλης Μαρινάκης συνεχίζουν να βρίσκονται στο πλευρό των κατοίκων του Αρκαλοχωρίου, με τη στήριξη της περιοχής να συνεχίζεται και μετά τον καταστροφικό σεισμό του 2021.
Με αφορμή την έναρξη της νέας σχολικής χρονιάς, η ΠΑΕ Ολυμπιακός και ο πρόεδρος του συλλόγου προσέφεραν σχολικές τσάντες και σχολικά είδη στα παιδιά των Δημοτικών Σχολείων της Ιεράς Μητρόπολης Αρκαλοχωρίου, Καστελλίου και Βιάννου.
Η πρωτοβουλία έχει στόχο να στηρίξει τους μαθητές της σεισμόπληκτης περιοχής και να τους προσφέρει τα απαραίτητα εφόδια για τη νέα σχολική χρονιά.
Η σχέση του Ολυμπιακού με το Αρκαλοχώρι έχει ξεκινήσει από τις πρώτες ημέρες μετά τον ισχυρό σεισμό του 2021. Ο Βαγγέλης Μαρινάκης και η «ερυθρόλευκη» ΠΑΕ είχαν κινηθεί άμεσα για την κάλυψη των αναγκών των κατοίκων, ενώ στη συνέχεια προχώρησαν και σε σημαντικές δωρεές για τις σχολικές υποδομές της περιοχής. Συγκεκριμένα, το 2021 είχε ανακοινωθεί η δωρεά σχολικών αιθουσών για το Γενικό Λύκειο Αρκαλοχωρίου και το Γενικό Λύκειο Καστελλίου.
Το «ευχαριστώ» της Μητρόπολης
Ο Αρχιμανδρίτης Αγαθάγγελος Γιανναράκης αναφέρθηκε στη νέα προσφορά και ευχαρίστησε τον Βαγγέλη Μαρινάκη για τη διαχρονική στήριξή του.
«Θα ήθελα να ευχαριστήσω τον κύριο Βαγγέλη Μαρινάκη, τον πρόεδρο της ΠΑΕ Ολυμπιακός, διότι εκτός από την Μητρόπολη Πειραιώς την οποία στηρίζει με γενναιότητα, έχει δείξει την αγάπη του και στη δική μας Μητρόπολη, τη σεισμόπληκτη Μητρόπολη, που μας έχει βοηθήσει αρκετά.
Τον ευχαριστούμε που έδωσε τη δυνατότητα στα παιδιά των περιοχών μας να έχουν τα σχολικά τους είδη για τη νέα τους σχολική χρονιά. Να ευχηθούμε όλοι στον Βαγγέλη Μαρινάκη καλή δύναμη και να συνεχίσει να προσφέρει τη βοήθειά του στη Μητρόπολη μας».

title: Czech pensions to rise in January, with CZK 2,000 bonus also planned
content:
People receiving Czech pensions will get an increase from January, with the average old-age pension set to rise by CZK 304 a month to CZK 22,196. The government also wants to pay pensioners a one-time CZK 2,000 bonus, though that payment has not yet become law.
The cabinet approved the annual pension adjustment Monday as it considered next year’s state budget. Labor and Social Affairs Minister Aleš Juchelka said the monthly increase amounts to about 1.4 percent for someone receiving the average old-age pension.
The two measures have different statuses: the government has approved the January adjustment by regulation, while the bonus requires Parliament to pass an amendment to the pension insurance law. Finance Minister Alena Schillerová said the government plans to add it to legislation already before the lower house.
How much will individual pensions rise?
Every pension includes a basic amount and an earnings-related amount. From January, the basic amount will rise by CZK 270 to CZK 5,170 a month for all recipients. The earnings-related portion will increase by 0.2 percent.
For someone receiving the average old-age pension, that second increase works out to about CZK 34. Together, the two changes bring the average monthly rise to CZK 304. Individual increases will vary because the earnings-related portion differs from person to person.
Minimum pension amounts will also rise. The new minimum will be CZK 5,170 for old-age pensions and third-degree disability pensions, according to the Labor Ministry. The minimums for other disability, survivor and orphan pensions will increase by differing amounts.
Why a one-time payment?
Juchelka said the government chose an additional single payment because the average pension is expected to fall relative to the average gross wage next year. The ministry projects that ratio will decline from 41.9 percent to 40.2 percent.
“We agreed in the coalition that pensioners will receive an additional CZK 2,000 as a one-time payment,” Juchelka said, according to iDNES.cz. He argued that a single payment would put less lasting pressure on the budget than adding the same support to monthly pensions.
The ministry estimates the annual pension increase will cost CZK 10.3 billion in 2027. About CZK 9.2 billion comes from raising the basic amount, with another CZK 1.1 billion for the increase to earnings-related amounts above the legal minimum.
Pensioners can expect the approved monthly increase in January. Whether and when they receive the separate CZK 2,000 payment depends on the proposed legal change passing Parliament.

title: Fenómeno El Niño: Gobierno tiene estrategia integral para garantizar seguridad alimentaria
content:
El ministro de Desarrollo Agrario y Riego, Marco Vinelli, informó hoy que el Gobierno maneja una estrategia integral para garantizar la seguridad alimentaria en el país ante el impacto del fenómeno El Niño.


"Venimos monitoreando el tema de la producción de alimentos y podemos informar a la población que al mes de setiembre tenemos un ingreso regular de alimentos", declaró en el programa Andina al Día del Canal Andina Online.
Por ejemplo, dijo que en la ciudad capital, en donde se monitorean los mercados mayoristas de Lima, siguen entrando un promedio de 7,000 toneladas a 8,000 toneladas de alimentos todos los días.
"No hay una disminución en el flujo de los alimentos", enfatizó el titular del Ministerio de Desarrollo Agrario y Riego (Midagri).
Monitoreo permanente
Vinelli afirmó que este trabajo de monitoreo continuará en las próximas semanas con el fin de determinar si es que hay algún tipo de afectación en la disponibilidad de alimentos.
"Hasta el momento no se ha presentado ningún problema de disponibilidad de alimentos", puntualizó Vinelli.
En Lima
En el caso específico de Lima comentó que hay otras cuatro vías alternas para asegurar el paso de alimentos si la Carretera Central llegara a verse afectada.
"Si se corta la Panamericana Sur, o la Panamericana Norte, lo que hay que hacer es cabotaje con los buques que tiene la Marina de Guerra del Perú para que los alimentos puedan llegar a la ciudad. El sector privado también está ofreciendo sus servicios de cabotaje para el traslado de alimentos", dijo.
"Estamos viendo toda esa parte logística de tal manera que funcione bien y que el impacto del fenómeno El Niño sea lo menor posible porque de todas maneras habrá impactos", subrayó el ministro.
Detalló que la Marina de Guerra ha puesto a disposición cinco buques para atender este tema.
Trabajo coordinado
De otro lado, mencionó que para atender los desastres, o las emergencias que puedan ocurrir, se está trabajando con Indeci y el sector privado en la compra de alimentos no perecibles para poder atender a las familias que se vean afectadas.

"Tenemos una capacidad de almacenamiento de 7,000 toneladas preservadas para que se puedan guardar ahí diversos bienes de ayuda humanitaria, de tal manera que si ocurre un desborde, o si se afectan algunas familias, esos alimentos puedan trasladarse para atender rápidamente con alimentación, agua, medicamentos, entre otros.
Además, dijo que para ver el tema de salud se dispone de tres hospitales de campaña ubicados en Tumbes, Piura y Lambayeque. "El objetivo es que si una persona ve afectada su salud pueda atenderse rápidamente", anotó.

title: WERBUNG - Auf Kasse: Medizinische Hauskrankenpflege
content:
Nach einer OP oder bei notwendiger Wundpflege kann die medizinische Hauskrankenpflege für daheim verordnet werden. Das erspart mühsame Ambulanzbesuche.
Zuckerkrank! Das war ein Riesenschock für die 89-jährige Herta M., als der Hausarzt bei ihr „Diabetes mellitus“ diagnostizierte. Und dann auch noch eine akute Überzuckerung im Dezember 2024.
Glück im Unglück: Obwohl Herta M. auch bei laufender Behandlung im Spital ihr diabetischer Fuß noch zu schaffen machte, konnte sie bereits nach wenigen Tagen wieder nach Hause. Der entlassende Arzt hatte ihr nämlich eine „Medizinische Hauskrankenpflege“ verordnet. Herta M. hat zuvor noch nie von dieser – für sie kostenlosen – Leistung gehört. Noch bevor sie das Krankenhaus verließ, organisierte das Entlassungsmanagement bereits ganz unbürokratisch die medizinische Hauskrankenpflege der FSW-Pflege- und Betreuungsdienste für sie.
Medizinisch-pflegerische Versorgung im eigenen Zuhause
„Ich war so erleichtert, wieder nach Hause zu können. Am liebsten bin ich einfach in meinen eigenen vier Wänden“, sagt sie. Gleichzeitig beschäftigte Herta M. die Sorge um ihre Wunde: „Ich hatte Angst, dass sich etwas entzündet oder ich etwas falsch mache.“
Diese Sorge war rasch beseitigt: Bereits am Tag nach der Entlassung kam eine diplomierte Pflegefachkraft zu ihr nach Hause. Ihr Fuß, bei dem durch den ständig erhöhten Blutzuckerspiegel die Nerven- und Blutgefäße geschädigt waren, konnte so einfach in ihrer Wohnung in Simmering professionell behandelt werden: ohne mühsame Fahrten in die Ambulanz und lange Wartezeiten! Dreimal pro Woche wurde ihre Wunde professionell versorgt und der Heilungsverlauf kontrolliert.
Rasch merkte die Seniorin, dass sich die schmerzhaften und schlecht abheilenden Wunden dank der medizinisch-pflegerischen Versorgung besserten. Das spürte sie auch durch mehr Lebensqualität und Beweglichkeit.
„Es war ein gutes Gefühl zu wissen, dass jemand kommt, auf den ich mich verlassen kann und dass ich mit meinen Sorgen nicht allein bin“, erinnert sich die Seniorin.
Medizinische Hauskrankenpflege – wie bekomme ich sie?
Wenn der Arzt – so wie bei Herta M. – einen Bedarf für Pflegeleistungen erkennt, kann er medizinische Hauskrankenpflege verordnen. Hinter der medizinischen Hauskrankenpflege steht ein Team speziell geschulter Pflegeexpert:innen. Sie übernehmen die Versorgung komplexer Wunden, Stoma-, Fistel- oder Katheterpflege, sorgen für die Verabreichung von speziellen Injektionen bzw. Infusionen oder künstlicher Ernährung. So erhalten Patient:innen nach einem Krankenhausaufenthalt – oder sogar stattdessen – eine medizinisch-pflegerisch hochwertige Versorgung direkt zu Hause.
Die Anordnung gilt zunächst für maximal 28 Kalendertage und ist bei Bedarf nach chefärztlicher Bewilligung verlängerbar. Die Kosten dafür trägt der jeweilige Sozialversicherungsträger.
Einfach medizinische Hauskrankenpflege vereinbaren
Wer in Wien wohnt und eine solche Anordnung erhalten hat, meldet sich am besten direkt bei der Mobilen Hauskrankenpflege des FSW (werktags von 7:30 – 15:30 Uhr unter 01/24 5 24 – 30 300) und vereinbart einen persönlichen Besuchstermin daheim. Dann kommt die professionelle Pflegekraft zum vereinbarten Zeitpunkt vorbei und übernimmt die notwendige Versorgung. Das erspart langwierige Arzt- oder Ambulanzbesuche bzw. stationäre Aufenthalte und gibt den Betroffenen die Sicherheit, zu Hause bestens versorgt zu sein.

title: No Albert Sabin, 19 modalidades esportivas ajudam o colégio a entrar no top 5 do Enem em SP
content:
(Divulgação)
Redatora
Publicado em 18 de setembro de 2026 às 14h03.
O Colégio Albert Sabin está entre as cinco melhores escolas de São Paulo no ranking do Enem. O resultado não vem só da sala de aula: a instituição mantém um dos maiores complexos esportivos e culturais da capital paulista, distribuído em um campus de 25.000 m², com 19 modalidades entre esporte e atividades artísticas oferecidas aos alunos.
A escola foi fundada por um empreendedor de origem simples, que construiu a instituição como forma de oferecer a outros as oportunidades que teve ao longo da vida.
Esse histórico atravessa a cultura do colégio junto a um segundo eixo, descrito pela gestão pedagógica como busca constante pelo aperfeiçoamento, não como um destino a ser alcançado.
Os alunos do Albert Sabin cumprem um núcleo comum de disciplinas, mas têm acesso a uma gama de atividades eletivas e extracurriculares que variam conforme o perfil de cada um. A diferença em relação a outras escolas está na forma como esse leque é oferecido: as atividades esportivas e culturais fazem parte do currículo, sem cobrança adicional das famílias.
Alunos relatam que o apoio da escola para participar de olimpíadas de conhecimento e de aulas com conceitos que chegam a ser de nível universitário fez diferença na trajetória escolar, especialmente nas modalidades esportivas.
O resultado, segundo a gestão pedagógica, é que cada estudante constrói uma trajetória própria, misturando esporte, cultura e formação acadêmica. Os benefícios vão além do desenvolvimento físico e motor: a escola aposta no ganho de competências socioemocionais como trabalho em equipe, tolerância à frustração, resiliência e autorregulação.
Esse retorno apareceu nos depoimentos de alunos aprovados em vestibulares ao final de 2025. Segundo a gestão pedagógica, foi comum ouvir desses estudantes que o esporte os ensinou a trabalhar sob pressão, gerir tempo e lidar com o erro, exatamente as demandas de uma prova como o Enem.
Ao lado do esporte, o colégio organiza sua proposta pedagógica em torno de outros dois pilares. O primeiro é o multilinguismo: a formação em uma ou duas línguas estrangeiras, a depender do interesse do aluno, pensada para preparar o estudante para um contexto profissional globalizado.
O segundo é o uso da tecnologia, tratado pela escola como elemento central para a vida pessoal, acadêmica, profissional e cidadã dos alunos. A orientação não é apenas usar ferramentas digitais, mas fazê-lo de forma ética e com capacidade de análise crítica sobre o impacto da tecnologia na sociedade.
No ensino médio, o colégio estrutura um núcleo de projetos que passa por Steam (ciência, tecnologia, engenharia, arte e matemática) na primeira série e por iniciação científica na segunda. Os alunos de Steam apresentam um pitch para uma banca avaliadora; os de iniciação científica seguem o modelo TED de apresentação.
Uma aluna descreve o projeto de iniciação científica como o momento em que percebeu qual carreira queria seguir, e cita também a experiência com um musical escolar como uma das vivências que mais contribuíram para sua formação pessoal.
A construção do projeto de vida passa por autoconhecimento e pelo exercício de escolha, e é reforçada por oficinas eletivas de orientação profissional, nas quais o aluno se inscreve por interesse e passa por dinâmicas voltadas a essa decisão.
Na preparação para os vestibulares, a escola apresenta aos alunos o formato das provas mais concorridas, promove simulados e usa análise de dados, individual e coletiva, para acompanhar o desempenho de cada turma. Para os estudantes, essa preparação vai além do conteúdo: é entender como fazer a prova.
Para a gestão pedagógica, um currículo que desenvolve repertório e competências é condição necessária, mas não suficiente. Também é preciso preparar o estudante para a demanda emocional e física de provas que chegam a durar cinco horas e que exigem resiliência, persistência e autorregulação.
O colégio mantém uma assessoria de internacionalização que orienta alunos interessados em universidades no exterior, incluindo cartas de recomendação e o processo burocrático de documentos e traduções.
A escola também oferece, todos os anos, possibilidades de summer camps fora do Brasil, sempre articulados a algum aprendizado complementar.
Para vários alunos, a passagem pelo colégio marcou a trajetória de forma definitiva, ao ponto de dizerem que não sabem o que teria sido de sua formação sem essa experiência.
Para a escola, essa é a lógica que sustenta todo o projeto pedagógico: formar pessoas capazes de realizar seus próprios planos e, ao mesmo tempo, contribuir para a construção de uma sociedade melhor.

A trajetória do Colégio Albert Sabin é o foco deste episódio da série documental Educação e Futuro, produção original da EXAME que investiga os bastidores, a infraestrutura e as metodologias de instituições de ensino que preparam estudantes para o mercado de trabalho e para a vida acadêmica. O episódio completo está disponível no canal oficial da EXAME no YouTube.

title: International Day Of Peace: Gurudev Sri Sri Ravi Shankar Meets Former Nⱥxalites Embracing Rehabilitation And New Beginnings
content:
For 28 years, Giridhar Tumreti lived in the forests of Gadchiroli, eventually becoming a State Committee member and leader of the Maoist movement. He witnessed dozens of comrades die, including 40 who were killed in an encounter in 2018, and at times carried their bodies on his shoulders.
One of the first to surrender to the Gadchiroli Police in the presence of Maharashtra Chief Minister Shri Devendra Fadnavis, Giridhar now speaks about those years from a different place in his life. He says some people believe former cadres are not good people, but “Gurudev welcomed us first” and treated them with respect. “When Gurudev spoke about us that way, it healed us,” says Giridhar.
Anil, another former cadre, recalls the guilt of a conflict in which “what we were doing with weapons killed thousands of people.” During his first Sudarshan Kriya session, he cried uncontrollably as memories of violence, deaths and the resulting grief resurfaced. “That feeling of guilt was there. How can we correct that? So much violence has happened.
So many people have been killed. What can we do for those families? We can’t do anything for those families anymore, whether it was the police or our own companions.” Anil said he had been battling depression for two years. But after coming to the Ashram, he said, “I realised more clearly that the life I had chosen was for the people. I realised that I can continue that work for the rest of my life. I don’t fear for my future anymore.”
A New Chapter Begins
Around 100 rehabilitated former Naxalites 60 men and 40 women from Gadchiroli travelled to The Art of Living International Center for a three-day Happiness Program and an interaction with Gurudev Sri Sri Ravi Shankar. The initiative was jointly undertaken by Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited, Lloyds Infinite Foundation and the Gadchiroli district police administration.
The programme seeks to help participants release the weight of their past, rebuild self-confidence and emotional resilience, and rediscover a sense of belonging and possibility after years of conflict.
For many who spent almost three decades inside a conflict, life after surrender has been filled with questions. Rehabilitation remains a long process of learning how to inhabit ordinary life again how to relate to people, one’s own memories, family and work, and eventually to the future.
Rebels Meet Gurudev
During the interaction, Gurudev told them, “You all took up a cause in your life, that everyone should get equality. You stood against injustice in society.” Acknowledging their courage and sacrifice, he said, “You have this enthusiasm within you. You have sacrifice. But there is one thing that needs to be added—spirituality.”
Gurudev also told them, “There is a way to work for the country without weapons. You are good people. Your path was wrong. I want you, your families to be happy, your children to go to school, we’ll work towards it together.” He later shared, “You do not have to leave your homes and families to bring change. Live within society, work for change, and take others along with you.”
Sushila said, “If I had met Gurudev earlier, I would never have gone into the forest or joined the Naxalite group.” After years of rain, heat, cold, hunger and the constant fear of firing, she said that meeting Gurudev and learning from him had brought a change she could feel within herself: “my body and mind have become better.”
Savita said, “If Gurudev had met us earlier, we would have found the right path sooner.” For her, a Guru was someone who could help one see what is right and what is wrong.
Giridhar recalled Gurudev telling them, “This Ashram belongs to you. Consider it your home. Whatever problems you have, you can leave them here.”
Rehabilitation Through Belonging
The initiative builds on a significant rehabilitation process in Gadchiroli, where more than 800 people have abandoned the path of violence and returned to the mainstream between 2005 and 2026.
Sandeep Patil, Inspector General of Police, Anti-Naxal Operations, Maharashtra, said the programme aims to help surrendered cadres overcome the bitterness accumulated through decades of conflict and become self-reliant. He said, “The purpose of this programme was that these surrendered cadres had been wandering in the jungle for 25–30 years.
There were many murders. So, to get rid of the bitterness in their minds towards society, we need an environment where they can go and become self-reliant. I feel that Bangalore, The Art of Living, was the best environment for that,” adding that regular Sudarshan Kriya and meditation practice would continue in Gadchiroli.
“I have always believed in The Art of Living and Guruji’s ability to connect with people and transform them,” shared Shri B Prabhakaran, MD, Lloyds Metals and Energy Ltd.
The Logical Indian Perspective
The journey of these former Naxalites shows the difficult transition from years of conflict to life after surrender. The interaction at The Art of Living International Center placed emphasis on respect, belonging and the possibility of rebuilding lives after decades spent in the forests.
For people carrying memories of deaths, violence, guilt and separation from ordinary life, rehabilitation is not limited to leaving the path of violence; it also involves learning to reconnect with family, society, work and their own future.
The meeting became a moment of profound human connection, with mutual respect between Gurudev and the former rebels. For those who had spent years in the forests without the security of a home or certainty about what tomorrow would bring, the assurance of having a place to belong carried significance.
There was no interrogation about the past. No demand to prove themselves worthy of a new beginning. Just an open door, and the quiet assurance that they could finally put their burdens down.
Also Read: International Youth Day: How Art of Living Helped Revive Hope for Manipur’s Chinlalchoi

title: Why are pensions in Abkhazia so low? Officials explain
content:
Why are pensions in Abkhazia so low? Officials explain
A 71-year-old resident of Abkhazia Marina Kachubeevna recently submitted documents to apply for Russian citizenship. Without a Russian passport, she cannot receive a Russian pension, which is relatively generous by local standards.
Her Abkhaz pension, which totals 6,000 roubles [$65] a month including all basic payments and supplements, is not enough to live on. So the woman has to continue working to have money of her own.
“I have wonderful children. My son and daughter-in-law never refuse me anything. When I started having health problems last year, they took full responsibility for paying for my medicines and doctors.
But every time I have to ask them for money for the pharmacy or basic personal needs, I feel uncomfortable. I don’t want to be a burden. At 71, I want to remain independent and be able to buy even small gifts for my grandchildren myself, without having to ask my children for the money,” Marina Kachubeevna says.
This desire to ease the financial burden on her family is the only reason she decided to apply for Russian citizenship.
Intergenerational solidarity and the reality of pension payments
The story of Marina Kachubeevna reflects broader systemic trends in Abkhazia’s social welfare system.
At present, around 33,000 people receive the basic old-age pension of 6,000 roubles. As the chairman of the republic’s Pension Fund, Denis Gularia, acknowledges, this amount falls far short of what is needed to live on.
However, Gularia points to a traditional model of social support in Abkhaz society, based on assistance from relatives.
“There is such a concept as intergenerational solidarity: children should help their parents. Of course, some pensioners do not have children, but this is the kind of society we have. Neighbours help each other as much as they can.
We constantly hear criticism directed at us. We hear it and understand it. But people have to help each other,” the Pension Fund chairman says.
He also stresses that the number of people receiving additional domestic payments continues to grow:
“The number of people receiving supplementary payments is approaching 17,000 and will continue to grow. Many of our citizens no longer have enough Soviet-era work experience to qualify for a pension from Russia’s Social Fund, so they will receive only our payments. We will try to find the funds to increase these payments in the future.”
41,000 workers supporting 50,000 pensioners
The main obstacle to a significant increase in pensions is the imbalance between the number of officially employed residents and the number of people receiving pensions and benefits.
According to statistics, Abkhazia has a working-age population of 144,000. Of these, around 40,000–41,000 people officially work and pay social insurance contributions. Meanwhile, around 51,000 people receive supplementary payments or pensions.
“With this ratio, high pensions are simply impossible. The remaining part of the population, around 100,000 people, work but do not contribute to the Pension Fund,” Gularia explains.
Commercial businesses also create an additional problem by avoiding full payment of social insurance contributions:
“Unfortunately, not everyone declares their full salary. The minimum salary in commercial organisations here is 20,000 roubles [$215]**. But if someone earns more, employers and employees often agree to declare only the minimum.
People themselves should have an interest in ensuring that social insurance contributions are paid. Remember, the contributions made by the 40,000 people who work today support the entire older generation.”
Reforms, collection orders and individual records
To change the situation, the Pension Fund plans to introduce individual records for insurance contributions and tighten fiscal discipline.
“A flat-rate system is unfair to those who pay honestly. One person pays contributions based on their actual salary, while another declares the minimum, yet they both receive the same pension. That is unfair.
Once we introduce individual records for insurance contributions, it will benefit people who plan to remain economically active: in addition to the basic 6,000 roubles, they will receive substantial payments based on the contributions recorded in their personal account,” Gularia says.
At the same time, the fund is actively working with employers who fail to meet their obligations. According to the chairman, the agency can issue collection orders when contributions are overdue. A collection order allows a bank to debit money from a payer’s account without prior consent. In 2025, the fund recovered 49.9 million roubles [around $537,000] in this way.
Some businesses also voluntarily repay old debts.
“We need to adopt legislation that strengthens the responsibility of managers and accountants who fail to submit reports on time,” Gularia says.
Re-registration for oversight and transparency
The re-registration of pensioners, which runs from 1 September to 1 December 2026, is another necessary step towards putting the system in order.
“There are cases when relatives do not always register a pensioner’s death promptly or submit the death certificate to social welfare offices. The money saved as a result of these checks will go into a fund for future increases in supplementary payments to the most vulnerable groups,” the official explains.
Apparently, bringing businesses out of the shadow economy, introducing individual records and ensuring that people pay their contributions properly offer the only way to ensure that, in a few years, pensioners such as Marina Kachubeevna can retire without financial worries, feel secure and afford to buy gifts for their grandchildren without having to work at the age of 71.
The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

title: Phillip Island removed foxes; little penguin colony grew from 12,000 to 40,000
content:
Phillip Island’s little penguins once faced a crisis that threatened to erase much of their presence from the island. By the 1980s, nine of its 10 penguin colonies had disappeared, while the final colony on the Summerland Peninsula was also under pressure from introduced predators, habitat loss and human activity. According to Phillip Island Nature Parks, a long-running conservation effort combining fox control, habitat restoration, scientific research and land rehabilitation helped reverse that decline. The surviving little-penguin population grew from about 12,000 in the mid-1980s to an estimated 40,000 today. The story, detailed in the organisation’s pest-control, research and history records, shows how protecting wildlife often requires more than removing a single threat—it demands sustained cooperation between scientists, governments, local communities and visitors. Read on to know more:
A predator that changed the island
Phillip Island, also known as Milawul, is famous for the nightly arrival of little penguins at the Penguin Parade. Yet the sight that attracts visitors today was once at risk of disappearing.
Red foxes were introduced to Phillip Island in the early 1900s. Over time, they became one of the most serious threats to the island’s wildlife. Little penguins are especially vulnerable because they spend much of their lives at sea but return to land to breed, moult and raise their chicks. Their nests are often located in burrows or sheltered areas close to the coast, where they can be exposed to predators.
Phillip Island Nature Parks describes foxes as the little penguins’ biggest threat on land. By the 1980s, nine of the island’s 10 penguin colonies had become extinct. The remaining colony on the Summerland Peninsula, which includes the Penguin Parade, was also under threat.
The decline was not caused by foxes alone. Research identified several other pressures, including habitat destruction, housing development, traffic near penguin colonies, fire and domestic pets. Together, these threats made it increasingly difficult for penguins to survive and breed successfully.
Warning signs from research
The island’s conservation response was shaped by research. Population studies conducted during the 1980s showed that the last remaining penguin colony could disappear by the late 1990s if existing threats continued.
That warning encouraged authorities and conservation groups to take action. The Penguin Protection Plan, announced in 1985, included scientific research, habitat management, a fox-control program and the gradual buyback of houses in the Summerland Estate.
The housing estate had been built within the penguins’ habitat. As houses, roads and associated infrastructure were removed, the land could be returned to a more natural condition. This was a major undertaking and required years of planning, funding and rehabilitation.
Phillip Island Nature Parks says the buyback and removal of the Summerland Estate continued for decades, as per reports. The final houses and infrastructure were removed in 2010, after which an ongoing rehabilitation program was established to help penguins and other wildlife thrive.
This approach recognised an important conservation principle: removing a predator is not enough if the habitat remains unsafe. Wildlife needs places to shelter, feed, breed and raise young without constant disturbance.
The campaign against foxes
Fox control began as a coordinated effort involving farmers, rangers and conservation workers. According to Phillip Island Nature Parks, more than 1,000 foxes were removed over a period of 20 years.
The organisation initiated a dedicated Fox Eradication Project in 2006. Rather than relying on one method, the project used an integrated approach involving different techniques to locate and remove foxes across the island.
The goal was ambitious. Instead of simply reducing fox numbers, conservation teams aimed to remove foxes from Phillip Island altogether. This was important because even a small number of predators could threaten vulnerable colonies and prevent other species from recovering.
The campaign required persistent monitoring. Rangers and other workers had to search for signs of foxes, respond to sightings and prevent the animals from re-establishing a population. The work also formed part of wider pest management on the island, including programs targeting feral and roaming cats and rabbits.
In 2017, Phillip Island was declared fox-free after an intensive 20-year eradication program. The campaign was supported by the Victorian Government, Penguin Parade visitors, the Penguin Foundation and the Helen Macpherson Smith Trust.
Habitat restoration made a difference
The recovery of the little penguins was closely connected to the restoration of their habitat.
The Summerland Peninsula had once been transformed by housing development and human activity. Removing the houses allowed conservation teams to rebuild a landscape better suited to wildlife. The rehabilitation work helped restore vegetation, reduce disturbance and create safer areas for nesting.
The return of natural habitat also benefited species beyond little penguins. Short-tailed shearwaters and other coastal birds use the island’s protected areas, while the fox-free environment later supported the reintroduction of eastern barred bandicoots.
In 2017, the same year Phillip Island was declared fox-free, researchers released eastern barred bandicoots onto the Summerland Peninsula. The area had been rehabilitated from a former housing estate into a natural environment that supported a thriving little-penguin colony and migratory short-tailed shearwaters.
This illustrates how conservation gains can extend across an ecosystem. Protecting one habitat can create opportunities for several threatened species, especially when predators are controlled and human disturbance is reduced.
From 12,000 to 40,000 penguins
Phillip Island Nature Parks reports that extensive conservation work helped increase the number of little penguins from approximately 12,000 in the mid-1980s to an estimated 40,000 today.
The figures represent more than a simple population increase. They reflect the combined effect of predator control, habitat restoration, reduced development pressure, scientific monitoring and community involvement.
The Penguin Parade also provides a useful way to monitor changes. Guides count the number of penguins crossing the beach each night, and annual averages can offer insight into population trends. These counts do not represent every penguin on the island, but they help researchers track changes in the colony over time.
Conservation teams also monitor breeding success by studying the number of chicks fledged per breeding pair at selected sites. This helps researchers understand not only how many penguins return to land, but also whether they are successfully reproducing.
Such long-term monitoring is essential because wildlife populations can change in response to food availability, disease, weather, marine conditions, human activity and other factors. Regular data collection allows managers to identify problems early and adjust conservation strategies.
Research continues on land and sea
Although the fox eradication campaign was a major achievement, the work of protecting little penguins has not ended.
Phillip Island Nature Parks says its researchers study penguins in both terrestrial and marine environments. This is necessary because little penguins spend around 80 per cent of their time at sea, even though they depend on land for breeding.
Researchers use GPS trackers and other devices to study where penguins travel for food. Tracking has shown that many penguins feed within 50 kilometres of the island’s colony, while some individuals travel farther during winter, including towards Portland in Victoria and Port Phillip Bay near Melbourne.
Understanding these movements helps scientists identify potential threats in the marine environment. Changes in ocean temperature, prey availability, pollution and human activity can all affect the penguins’ ability to find food.
Research projects also examine feeding hotspots by combining information about where penguins go, how much they eat and what prey they consume. This evidence can help guide future conservation decisions as marine ecosystems respond to environmental change.
A model for community-led conservation
Phillip Island’s recovery story shows that successful conservation rarely happens through one dramatic action. It is usually built through many years of practical work.
The fox eradication program required rangers, farmers, scientists, government agencies, conservation organisations and local residents to work towards the same goal. Visitors also contributed through tourism, with Phillip Island Nature Parks stating that visits help fund research and wildlife conservation.
The island’s history also highlights the importance of acknowledging the Bunurong people, the Traditional Owners of Milawul. Phillip Island Nature Parks recognises the continuing connection of the Bunurong to the landscape and describes its role in healing Country and supporting Traditional Owner involvement in decisions about Country.
The little penguins’ recovery is therefore not only a story about numbers. It is a story about restoring a damaged landscape, learning from scientific evidence and changing the way people share space with wildlife.
What the future depends on
The increase from 12,000 to 40,000 little penguins is encouraging, but it does not mean the species is permanently secure on Phillip Island. Conservation gains must be maintained.
Foxes must remain absent. Other introduced predators, including feral and roaming cats, require continued management. Roads, pets, fires, rubbish, human disturbance and habitat damage can still affect wildlife.
The penguins’ time at sea also creates challenges that cannot be solved entirely on land. Their food supply may be influenced by changing ocean conditions, climate change and human activity. That is why Phillip Island’s conservation program combines population counts, breeding studies, tracking and marine research.
The lesson from Phillip Island is clear: wildlife recovery becomes possible when threats are identified early and addressed consistently. A colony that once appeared destined to vanish has grown substantially because people chose to protect its habitat, remove its predators and continue monitoring its future.
For the little penguins returning to shore each evening, that long-term commitment has made the difference between disappearance and survival.

title: El pueblito del Perú que hará historia durante la visita del Papa León XIV
content:
La expectativa en el norte peruano ha alcanzado un nivel histórico. El distrito de Zaña, ubicado en la región Lambayeque, se prepara para convertirse en el epicentro de un acontecimiento sin precedentes. Por primera vez en la historia de las visitas pontificias al país, un Santo Padre detendrá su recorrido en una localidad rural para reencontrarse con la comunidad que acompañó de cerca sus años de servicio pastoral.
El anuncio de la llegada del papa León XIV ha conmovido a los habitantes de este emblemático distrito, quienes recuerdan con afecto y gratitud la época en que Robert Francis Prevost ejercía su labor obispal en la diócesis de Chiclayo. Entre preparativos litúrgicos y una profunda devoción popular, Zaña aguarda la llegada del vicario de Cristo con el orgullo de saber que su nombre quedará grabado en los anales de la Iglesia Católica.
Zaña: de diócesis histórica a destino pontificio
Zaña no es una tierra ajena a la historia religiosa del Perú. Fundada en la época colonial y bendecida por el paso de figuras ilustres como Santo Toribio de Mogrovejo, la localidad suma ahora un hito contemporáneo de escala internacional. La conexión de León XIV con esta tierra se consolidó durante su periodo como obispo de Chiclayo, etapa en la que caminó por sus calles, celebró la eucaristía en sus templos y conoció de primera mano las necesidades de sus familias.
Para el padre David Farfán, párroco del templo Santo Toribio de Mogrovejo, esta visita trasciende lo protocolar. Durante su participación en un documental del Arzobispado de Lima, el sacerdote destacó la singularidad de la elección papal: “Es la primerísima vez que un Santo Padre incluye dentro de las grandes metrópolis a un pueblito”. Este gesto visibiliza a las comunidades periféricas y descentraliza la agenda habitual de los viajes papales, enfocando la atención de la fe católica en los rincones más sencillos del país.
Los recuerdos y testimonios de la comunidad zañera
El impacto de la visita se vive con especial intensidad en las calles y hogares de Zaña. Los vecinos recuerdan las misas dominicales, las visitas pastorales a los caseríos más alejados y el compromiso social desplegado por Robert Francis Prevost antes de su elección como sumo pontífice. Durante su gestión pastoral, el hoy papa León XIV impulsó diversas iniciativas de apoyo humanitario y fortalecimiento comunitario, especialmente en momentos de adversidad climática y económica en la región norteña.
Los testimonios locales coinciden en calificar su trato como cercano, sencillo y acogedor. Para muchas familias, volver a ver al obispo que caminó a su lado, ahora vistiendo el blanco pontificio, representa una bendición y un motivo de profunda gratitud. Las agrupaciones parroquiales y los fieles organizan comités de bienvenida para recibir al pontífice con cantos, testimonios y expresiones culturales propias de la identidad afroperuana y criolla de la zona.
Fechas y detalles del itinerario de León XIV en el Perú
La visita oficial del papa León XIV al Perú está programada del 11 al 16 de noviembre. Durante esta jornada de seis días, el Santo Padre cumplirá un itinerario que combinara los encuentros multitudinarios en las principales urbes del país con paradas de profundo valor afectivo y espiritual, como la programada en la Región Lambayeque.
La llegada del pontífice al distrito de Zaña se perfila como uno de los momentos más conmovedores de su viaje pastoral. Se espera que durante su estancia comparta un mensaje de esperanza y fraternidad con los comuneros, agricultores y familias que marcaron su itinerario misionero en el norte del país. La logística local se coordina entre las autoridades regionales, la Policía Nacional y la Conferencia Episcopal Peruana para garantizar la seguridad de los miles de visitantes y peregrinos que se trasladarán hacia la zona.
Un mensaje de transformación y renovación fe
Más allá del fervor inicial y la cobertura mediática, la llegada de León XIV plantea un desafío para los habitantes de Lambayeque. Como señaló el padre David Farfán, el verdadero impacto de este acontecimiento dependerá de la recepción interior que la comunidad dé a la enseñanza del pontífice. La visita no solo busca dejar un recuerdo en la memoria colectiva, sino también impulsar una renovación espiritual y social orientada a la solidaridad, la justicia y la atención a los más vulnerables.
El pueblito de Zaña, con su riqueza histórica y sus ruinas coloniales, se alista para escribir uno de sus capítulos más memorables. Con la cuenta regresiva hacia el 11 de noviembre en marcha, la expectativa crece en cada rincón del distrito, donde la fe y la memoria de un pasado compartido se unen para dar la bienvenida al papa León XIV.

title: Building a Black Honors Community
content:
California State University, Sacramento
When Naomi Thrower was applying to college, she knew she wanted the historically Black college or university experience but hesitated to leave the community she had built in California, which does not have a traditional HBCU.
So she applied to HBCUs across the country, as well as to California State University, Sacramento, the state’s first Black-serving institution.
“Sacramento State is the only California school I applied to. The rest were all East Coast HBCUs,” Thrower said. “I do have family on the East Coast, but none I felt strongly connected with. So I would be leaving my family, my friends, the life I’ve built here, and that was a little nerve-racking.”
Now a fourth-year deaf studies major, Thrower has found a community in the university’s Black Honors College, a first-of-its-kind program that provides a culturally responsive curriculum and inclusive academic community for students focused on the Black experience.
“It really provided me with a strong social foundation,” said Thrower, who was part of the college's inaugural cohort in 2024. “I knew everybody in my cohort, so when I was in my classes, when we started for the first day, I was nervous, but I already saw familiar faces, and so the [Black Honors College] provided me with that community feel.”
A growing community: Originally announced in 2023, Sacramento State’s Black Honors College offers smaller, specialized general education classes and is open to students of all races and majors. It also provides dedicated mentorship, paid internships, residential living-learning options and scholarships. The model offers a window into what can happen when an honors college centers Black history, culture and experiences in its curriculum while emphasizing community and belonging.
The Black Honors College admits incoming first-year students each fall, while transfer students and continuing Sacramento State sophomores and juniors can apply each spring. Students must have a 3.5 GPA at the time of application and maintain a 3.0 GPA or higher to remain enrolled.
Boatamo Ati Mosupyoe, dean of students and chief academic officer at Sacramento State, said the college initially planned to admit only 50 students in fall 2024, but growing interest led it to admit 80. The fall 2025 class grew to 262 students; this year's class is 414 students, bringing the total enrollment to 914.
Mosupyoe attributes that growth in part to the environment the college has sought to create, one that emphasizes students’ strengths rather than approaching them from what she described as a deficit perspective.
“We are creating a welcoming environment to the students,” Mosupyoe said. “This program doesn’t look at the students as deficient, and we don’t subscribe to a deficit model. We look at the potential of what these students are going to do.”
Matthew Ward, vice president of strategic enrollment management and chief enrollment officer, said the Black Honors College has become part of a broader effort at the university to intentionally support Black students and celebrate Black culture.
“We have lots of students who think about HBCUs but have to consider traveling across the country to go to an institution where they’re going to find that Black joy, Black excellence, Black dignity,” Ward said. “From what I’ve seen, in terms of the broader growth … word travels fast. There is definitely among students and families and school districts and educational leaders a real focus on Sacramento because it’s doing something that’s against the grain.”
That sense of community appealed to Manuel Tellez, a transfer student who grew up in Sacramento’s Oak Park neighborhood. Entering Sacramento State as a first-generation student, Tellez said he knew he needed the guidance of a strong Black community to feel comfortable and push himself academically, which he found in the Black Honors College.
“The Black Honors College pushed me to the next level [and] held me to a higher standard,” Tellez said. “Ever since then, my GPA has climbed, and I’ve been comfortable with going to school.”
Leland O’Neal, assistant program coordinator for the Black Honors College, said another strength of the college is the range of students and experiences represented within its cohorts.
“The pace of expansion has surprised me a little bit, but in a grand way,” O’Neal said. “We have students in that cohort, like Manuel, who are transfer students, but we also have students coming in who are as old as 69 or students who are as young as 19. So I think you really get a diverse array of perspectives and experiences.”
Building a network: As the Black Honors College has grown, so have its student supports. The college now offers financial literacy workshops, access to an in-house licensed therapist and events that celebrate Black culture. Mosupyoe said the number of professors affiliated with the college has also grown from 20 when the college began to 30 today.
“We have a community of administrators, staff and professors who are helping us really make sure that we provide what we have promised to students,” Mosupyoe said.
For Thrower, that support has extended beyond the classroom. She now works as a student assistant for the college and in that capacity has helped organize programming with the nonprofit Black Deaf Project to connect and socialize with students. The experience ultimately led her to an internship with the organization.
“The first piece of advice I got before college was that your net worth is your network,” Thrower said. “The Black Honors College has been that foundational network hub. I know people all over campus, and if I don’t know where to find some information, I know that I can go to the Black Honors College and they can direct me towards somebody who can help.”
(Updated 9/23, 12:20 p.m. to reflect the total number of students in the college.)

title: 5 British schoolgirls, 14-15, build firebreak robot, represent UK globally
content:
Five schoolgirls from Kent, aged between 14 and 15, have built a robot with five-metre folding arms to help fight wildfires. Their work has earned them the chance to represent Great Britain at an international robotics competition in South Korea. The team from The Folkestone School for Girls, known as Team Meglabyte, designed the robot to clear dry plants and create paths that remove fuel from the spread of fires. The school's robotics club was only founded in 2024, but it has now been chosen to represent Great Britain at the FIRST Global Challenge in Incheon.
Designing a solution to growing wildfire risks
The international competition brings together student teams from more than 190 countries to work on major environmental and technology problems. This year's challenge focuses on preventing, controlling and recovering from wildfires in a warming world. For the competition, the Folkestone students designed an autonomous vehicle with long, folding arms that can clear paths up to five metres wide through dry vegetation. The system removes plants and other surface material that can fuel a fire, creating natural firebreaks that can slow the spread of flames without putting firefighters directly in danger.
According to a statement on the official website of The Folkestone School for Girls, the students have been working to improve the robot before the global competition: "The Folkestone School for Girls robotics team, Team Meglabyte, are thrilled to be representing Great Britain at the First Global Challenge in South Korea."
Working with local firefighters
The five students worked with professional firefighters to make sure their design could deal with the real conditions faced during wildfires. According to a report by Kent news outlet Shepway Vox, the students spoke with Kent Fire and Rescue Service during the early stages of the project. The firefighters helped them understand how wildfires spread across difficult terrain. Their advice led the team to focus on building a lightweight and stable robot that could extend its arms across uneven ground without tipping over. The students also used standard parts supplied by the competition organisers to program the robot's autonomous driving system. The software allows the machine to avoid obstacles, clear debris and work on its own in areas where thick smoke could make remote control difficult.
National selection and fundraising
The team's success comes only two years after the school's robotics program was created. Despite having less experience than some international teams, the Kent students won the national selection process and secured Great Britain's single place in the competition. To help pay for their trip to Incheon and the materials needed to build their robot, the team launched a public crowdfunding campaign. On their official Crowdfunder page, the students explained their goal of representing Britain and encouraging more girls to study science and technology: "Our aim is to inspire young girls across GB into STEM and globally raise awareness about this year's competition theme of wildfires. Each year a single robotics team from a school in Great Britain is sent to compete in a robotics competition on the global stage. This year, five girls from the all-girls state school Folkestone School for Girls have been selected to represent the nation in South Korea to compete with their robot. The girls need your help to get them to the competition!" The students are also using the opportunity to create outreach programs for primary schools. These projects will give younger pupils basic coding kits and lesson plans showing how engineering can be used to solve real environmental problems. The FIRST Global Challenge will take place in Incheon, South Korea, where the five Folkestone students will put their robot to the test against teams from countries around the world.

title: À Molenbaix, l’art contemporain s’invite dans les rues et les champs et attire des visiteurs de toute la Wallonie
content:
À Molenbaix, l'art contemporain s'invite dans les rues et les champs et attire des visiteurs de toute la Wallonie
Il reste deux semaines pour découvrir "Butor", la première biennale d'art contemporain en campagne. Dix-neuf artistes, entre champs et hameaux.
- Publié le 19-09-2026 à 12h01
Le centre du village et le hameau de Butor voient passer de nombreux visiteurs, depuis quelques semaines. Ils viennent de différents coins de Wallonie, mais aussi des Flandres et de France.
"Butor" et douceur
Marcher de la ferme d'Ecavée au centre du village permet de découvrir un sentier singulier, en céramique gravée de mots. "De Molenbeek à Molenbaix", "Ce chemin est celui de tous" ... Citadins et ruraux se souviennent de venelles, sentes, petites voies, ruelles, chemins de pavés et de liens. Les enfants apprécient particulièrement cette oeuvre de Various Artists, un collectif également auteur d'un totem et de quelques interventions insolites.
"C'est ma petite-fille !" annonce fièrement Christian Collie quand des visiteurs s'approchent du terrain de foot. Léa - en miroir - est peinte par Charlotte Beaudry sur bois chantourné, aux couleurs du club. La jeune footballeuse de quinze ans joue à présent à Avelgem, elle est de plus, vu son talent, reprise dans la sélection nationale des Jeunes à Mons. Son grand-père, qui évolua au Racing de Tournai, fait partie du comité de foot de Molenbaix.
Un pas plus loin, Raphaël De Coster a créé une "zone de rupture potentielle", en utilisant un cordeau. Ligne droites et penchées, tendues vers la cime d'une structure qui puise son énergie dans un geste géométrique résolu. Chemin du centre, Lise Duclaux a placé des affiches porteuses de slogans courts, limpides : "Nous ne sommes que les autres". L'église Saint-Ghislain abrite des recherches picturales de Charlotte Beaudry, un autel à sainte Rita (Jacques Charlier) et une étonnante sculpture de Maaerten Vanden Eynde : un tronc d'arbre scié, posé sur une ancienne balance en fonte. L'oeuvre interroge l'équilibre, la fragilité, la pesanteur.
Lieux et liens
"C'est un choc, ce jaillissement !", s'exclame Frédérique, venue de Lasne à la rencontre de l'exposition. Devant "La terre saigne", fontaine de Laurence Dervaux, elle évoque son réflexe de "juguler la plaie", "voir arriver une ambulance" "une énorme puissance suggestive" . "Des visiteurs parlent ici autant de vie que de mort, songeant aux guerres comme aux souffrances infligées à la planète", souligne Caroline, l'une des guides de l'exposition.
Des groupes et duos se croisent, échangeant leurs impressions à propos du parcours, de la campagne, des nombreuses haltes proposées. Aucun artiste n'est oublié dans les conversations, les précisions et questions. Les interventions en extérieur comme en intérieur ouvrent des perspectives, déclenchent la surprise, l'admiration, la réflexion collective. Et cette certitude d'être au coeur d'une approche que l'on dit contemporaine : l'intégration au paysage, à la nature, l'assurance d'une discrétion privilégiée, la présence du symbole et de la beauté.
"Butor", au départ de la ferme d'Ecavée à Molenbaix, du jeudi au dimanche, de 10h30 à 18h. Possibilité de visites guidées. Jusqu'au 4 octobre.

title: [한경에세이] 콩이가, 준우가, 옥분 씨가 행복한 추석
content:
AI 추천 뉴스




[한경에세이] 콩이가, 준우가, 옥분 씨가 행복한 추석
김미경 서울 은평구청장




우리 집에 선물처럼 새로운 가족이 찾아온 지도 어느덧 두 해가 흘렀다. 이름은 콩이, 풀네임은 ‘김콩’. 하얀 얼굴에 복슬복슬한 털, 까만 눈 두 개와 까만 코 하나. 처음 데려왔을 때 부모님께서 “콩만하게 작네!”라며 지어준 이름이다. 아침마다 내 방문을 긁으며 “앙!”하고 나를 깨우고, 매일 부모님과 함께 불광천을 산책하며 일상에 녹아든 녀석을 보면, 엄연히 콩이가 우리 집의 막내아들 같은 강아지라는 사실을 실감한다.
콩이와 함께 살면서 가족에 대해 새삼 생각하게 된다. 돌이켜보면 우리가 가족이라고 부르는 모습은 과거와 많이 달라졌다. 피로 맺어진 혈연만이 가족의 전부는 아니다. 말없이 곁을 지키는 반려동물도, 홀로 살아가지만 자신의 일상을 단단하게 꾸려가는 청년과 어르신도 우리 사회의 소중한 가족이다.
명절만 되면 마음 한구석이 묵직해지는 소식을 접한다. 연휴 기간이면 유기동물이 급증한다는 뉴스다. 또 따라붙는 이야기가 있다. 온 가족이 모이는 명절일수록 오히려 고립감을 느끼며 쓸쓸함을 견뎌야 하는 이웃의 이야기다. 구청장으로 현장을 누비다 보면 그런 이야기를 듣는다. “혼자 사는데 아플 때 돌봐줄 사람이 없어 걱정이에요.”, “홀로 계신 어르신이 외로움을 많이 타세요.”, “우리 강아지가 아플 때 마음 편히 맡길 곳이 있으면 좋겠어요.”
나는 행정이 살펴야 할 가족의 범위를 조금씩 넓혔다. 지난 2020년 서울시 최초로 ‘반려동물도 가족’이라는 개념을 행정에 도입해 전담 팀을 꾸렸다. 청년부터 중년, 어르신에 이르기까지 1인 가구와 자립준비청년이 혼자서 모든 어려움을 감당하지 않도록 돌봄 안전망도 촘촘히 살피고 있다. 행정이 해야 할 일은 누군가의 외로움이 혼자 감당해야 할 몫이 되지 않도록 곁을 내주는 것인지도 모른다.
실제로 나는 추석이 되면 이들의 삶터를 찾아간다. 어릴 때 엄마와 함께 장보기가 소원이었다는 자립준비청년과 시장에서 장을 보고, 전통과자를 만들어 관내 아동복지시설에 나누고, 대조동 청년주택의 공유주방에서 1인 가구 청년들과 명절 음식을 준비한다. 그럴 때면 행정이란 결국 하나의 삶을 들여다보는 일이라는 생각이 든다. “동생들과 함께 나누고 싶었어요”라고 수줍게 건넨 자립준비청년의 이 한마디 속에서 가족의 의미를 되새긴다. 따뜻한 음식을 함께 나누고 서로의 안부를 묻는 사람이 바로 식구이자 가족이 아닐까.
민족 대명절 추석이다. 이번 연휴만큼은 형태가 어떠하든 우리 주변의 그 누구도 소외되지 않았으면 좋겠다. 홀로 명절상을 차리며 쓸쓸해할지 모를 우리 동네 준우와 옥분 씨의 안부를 한 번 더 돌아보고 싶다. 사람뿐만 아니라 이웃집의 해피와 까미, 우리 집 막내 콩이까지, 저마다의 자리에서 따뜻한 한가위를 보내길 바란다. 우리 옆의 가족들을 들여다보고, 좀 더 마음을 쓰는 추석 말이다.

title: Mural of rapper Macklemore painted in Gaza after Ed Sheeran tour furore
content:
Mural of rapper Macklemore painted in Gaza after Ed Sheeran tour furore
- Artists in Gaza painted a mural of rapper Macklemore wrapped in a Palestinian flag to thank him for supporting Palestine after he was removed from Ed Sheeran's tour.
- Macklemore donated US$1 million from the tour to Gaza aid groups, sparking matching pledges from other celebrities and highlighting the need for sustained support.
- Gaza remains devastated with stalled reconstruction and ongoing humanitarian needs, as locals value celebrity solidarity for raising awareness and pushing for peace.
AI generated
GAZA/JERUSALEM – Artists in Gaza have painted a mural of Macklemore wrapped in a Palestinian flag on a huge slab of concrete in the ruins of Gaza City, after the US rapper was kicked off Ed Sheeran’s upcoming tour for calling for a “Free Palestine”.
The mural, on a slab that leans against ruined buildings surrounded by rubble, depicts the “Thrift Shop” rapper raising a fist in the air.
“Thank you for using your voice for Palestine,” it reads.
“We wanted to send a message to thank rapper Macklemore in this simple way,” said Anne Redwan, 26, who designed and painted the mural with fellow artist Qusai al-Helo.
“As an artist living under siege here in Gaza, we are waiting for support from anyone who can see (the) persecution we live under,” she said. “We can paint murals bigger than this to express our feelings.”
Macklemore, who has long supported Palestinian causes, was cut from British pop star Sheeran’s musical line-up over remarks on stage criticising Israel’s military assault in Gaza, which was launched after Hamas-led fighters attacked Israel in October 2023.
Sheeran said he was unable to keep Macklemore on the tour after stadium owners refused to let him appear. US billionaire Robert Kraft, owner of Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts where his New England Patriots American football team plays, said he had barred Macklemore from appearing there for anti-Semitism, which the rapper denies.
Nearly a year after a ceasefire ended major fighting in Gaza, reconstruction has yet to begin. Most buildings have been destroyed and more than two million residents are confined to around a third of the enclave’s territory, mostly in tents or crowded rooms in damaged buildings among the ruins.
A US-brokered plan to end the war has stalled, with negotiators failing to agree to conditions for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.
The furore over Sheeran’s tour has led to a series of pledges from those involved to send money. Macklemore said on Sept 16 he would donate his US$1 million (S$1.3 million) in net earnings from the tour to six aid groups supporting Gaza.
Kraft, in turn, said Sheeran had told him he would donate US$2 million for aid in the region and had asked him to match the pledge. Sheeran has not commented on any donations. Macklemore’s donation drew a matching US$1 million pledge from Ms Rachel, a popular children’s TV personality.
Aid agency officials said the boost in celebrity attention could help bring more support to Gaza, where nearly all residents rely on aid for food, water, medical care and shelter.
“But what’s really most important is that people who have been so generous keep fighting over a sustained time,” said Toby Fricker, a local official with UNICEF. “That’s why we really call for sustained support, not one-off peaks, but sustained.”
Hussein Murtaja, who runs a Gaza humanitarian group that provides mental health support to children, said Macklemore’s solidarity matters more than the money he donated.
“When artistes of this stature, with this many followers or fans, all come to know more about the cause, and support reaching a political solution, support achieving peace for the people of Gaza... That means a great deal to us.” REUTERS

title: El alcohol está de capa caída y en Euskadi no creen que sea impedimento para divertirse: llegan las barras "light" a Bizkaia
content: Hace más de un año ya apuntábamos a una gran crisis del alcohol entre los jóvenes. Más allá de la presión social, esa vieja aliada, el bebercio tradicional está disminuyendo entre las generaciones actuales. Bajo este contexto, Bizkaia acaba de estrenar un híbrido: la discoteca de siempre, con su barra habitual, y al lado, otra barra a 0,0 grados. Mismo precio, misma pista, cero alcohol. La idea llega meses después de que abriera en Hernani la primera discoteca silenciosa de Euskadi, con 200 auriculares y tres canales de música por colores. Dos experimentos y un mismo cliente de fondo: alguien que ya no bebe, o bebe bastante menos, que hace quince años. Menos borracheras. Según la última Encuesta sobre Uso de Drogas en Enseñanzas Secundarias, el 51,8% de los adolescentes españoles ha bebido en el último mes, la cifra más baja desde 1998. Las chicas beben más que los chicos, por cierto. O eso dicen las estadísticas. Lo que está claro es que las borracheras han caído al 17,2% y el consumo en atracón, al 24,7%: ambos, mínimos históricos. En Euskadi la tendencia se repite: los datos del Gobierno Vasco confirman que el descenso es más notable entre los menores de 34 años, tanto chicos como chicas. Salir, beber, el rollo de siempre. Aquí llega el dato dañino: quien más bebe de forma arriesgada no es la juventud, sino la gente de 35 a 54 años, con un 32% en niveles de riesgo, frente al 17% de los menores de 35. En Bilbao, vecinos de Abando e Indautxu llevan tiempo señalando a los “cuarentones” como el colectivo más conflictivo del ocio nocturno, por encima de los jóvenes que ocupan las salas los fines de semana. El txikiteo pierde parroquia. La tradición vasca de ir haciendo chiquitos (tomar chatos o vasos pequeños de vino) de bar en bar resiste, pero con menos público. Según la Asociación de Hostelería de Bizkaia, la población joven se ha reducido prácticamente a la mitad respecto a hace quince años. Una “sangría” que golpea directamente la facturación nocturna. El ocio se desplaza hacia el tardeo, que representa el 26% de la facturación en hostelería nacional, y el botellón, inexistente antes de los 2000, que se lleva una parte importante del gasto que antes iba para discotecas. Es cancerígeno, punto. Un recordatorio, porque la ciencia no deja mucho margen para el matiz aquí. La Agencia Internacional para la Investigación del Cáncer, brazo de la OMS, clasifica el alcohol como carcinógeno del grupo 1 desde 1988: la misma categoría que el tabaco, el amianto o la radiación. Está vinculado a al menos siete tipos de cáncer (boca, faringe, laringe, esófago, hígado, colon-recto y mama) y provoca, según la propia IARC, el 4% de todos los cánceres diagnosticados en el mundo, más de 740.000 casos y 401.000 muertes al año. El mecanismo es conocido: el etanol se transforma en acetaldehído, un cancerígeno en sí mismo, y además genera inflamación y estrés oxidativo. La OMS recuerda que no existe un nivel de consumo seguro. Esa copa de vino diaria que durante años se vendió como cardiosaludable es mercadotecnia. En Xataka Madrid se ha llenado de "fiestas de dopamina": se acabó el alcohol, llegan las ensaladas y los baños de hielo Bailar en silencio. El otro empujón viene de la ley. España restringe la música en muchos locales a partir de las diez de la noche, y algunos bares vascos han resuelto el problema cambiando altavoces por cascos inalámbricos: la fiesta sigue, pero desde la calle no se oye nada. El bar de Hernani que lo estrenó reconoce que la medida, pensada solo para cumplir la normativa, acabó siendo su mejor reclamo comercial. Demasiado ruido. El Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica, la cual publica los Mapas Estratégicos de Ruido, que cruzan tráfico, industria y ocio nocturno calle a calle, no dejan bien parada a España: es el segundo país más ruidoso del mundo, solo por detrás de Japón, y más de 12 millones de personas soportan niveles por encima de los 65 decibelios que la OMS marca como límite aceptable. Barcelona y Madrid figuran entre las 20 ciudades con más contaminación acústica del planeta. Y hay coste sanitario: más de 1.000 muertes prematuras y 4.000 hospitalizaciones al año en España por exposición al ruido, según la Agencia Europea de Medio Ambiente, más dos millones de personas con problemas para conciliar el sueño. Y el ocio nocturno —bares, discotecas y botellón— concentra cerca del 28% de las denuncias vecinales por ruido, justo el frente que los cascos inalámbricos de Hernani intentan aliviar. Silencio también es accesibilidad. Bajar el volumen tiene, además, otra lectura: entre el 60% y el 90% de las personas con TEA presentan hipersensibilidad a sonidos fuertes y luces intermitentes. En Reino Unido, Disco Neurotico nació precisamente para eso: un local ideado por y para clubbers neurodivergentes —autismo, TDAH, TEPT— hartos de pistas abarrotadas, imprevisibles y sin vías de escape. En España, el proyecto Rumbo de Autismo España lleva años catalogando ocio con estímulo reducido. Nadie ha vendido la barra 'light' de Bizkaia como un recurso de accesibilidad, pero encaja. En Xataka A la pregunta de cuántos bares hay en España, este mapa desmonta mitos y reafirma algunos excesos Haciendo números. Si crece la cerveza sin alcohol, la pista es clara. La coctelería se ha puesto las pilas y las bebidas espirituosas sin alcohol han duplicado su volumen en España, con un crecimiento del 17% anual y un 64% acumulado desde 2021, según la Federación de Espirituosos. Y esto se imbrica con cierta audiencia: el 79% de la generación Z sigue saliendo a bares al menos una vez por semana, 8 puntos por encima de la media, aunque pidiendo menos birra y más cócteles, incluidos los de cero grados. Fiestear, versión 2026. Se bebe menos, pero el alcohol sigue funcionando como salvoconducto social en muchos ambientes de fiesta. Este tipo de iniciativas sacan al alcohol del centro de la ecuación como excusa obligatoria para socializar. Discotecas de Bizkaia como Backstage, en la calle Uribitarte número 8, lo han entendido: una barra sin alcohol junto a la de siempre no ahuyenta clientes, suma. El txikiteo de toda la vida convive ahora con auriculares, mocktails y una generación que prefiere recordar el sábado al día siguiente. title: UN Reports Over 68,000 Gain Healthcare Access in Nangarhar and Laghman with Italy’s Support
content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has announced that, with financial support from the Italian government, thousands of families in Nangarhar and Laghman provinces have gained access to essential primary healthcare services.
